Decision engineering · The short version

In brief: what AI needs before you let it act

One major thunderstorm, one airline and more code than a business reader should have to see. This page is the five-minute summary of the nine posts that follow, written for business leaders. If you want the technical underpinnings, go straight to the posts.

The short version

The core argument

Getting an AI agent to make a good decision is hard. Getting hundreds of them to act without causing an incident you have to explain to the board is harder. Right now, very few enterprises can prove who authorized an agent's actions, why the agent took that action and what it broke next. The whole series comes down to one sentence: every consequential business decision should have one verifiable record that connects its context, its authority, its execution and its outcome, whether a person, a rule, a model or an AI agent made it.

Decision engineering is the discipline that produces that record.

Throughout this series, I use one fictional scenario to make the ideas concrete: a thunderstorm at an airline's main hub that strands thousands of passengers.

Why this is now your problem

Automated decisions are not new; credit scoring has run on them for decades. What is new is how much AI now does on its own. A wrong answer in a chat window was corrected by whoever read it, usually with a sigh. A wrong action that rebooks passengers or releases payments takes effect before anyone reviews it, so the controls have to work before the action, not after. Somewhere in your organization AI already acts. The question is how to let it make bigger decisions without learning about its mistakes from a customer, an auditor or the finance team.

Two costs you are already paying

Decision latency is the time from something happening in the business to the action being confirmed: the passenger rebooked, the payment released. Every team measures its own slice, and nobody owns it end to end.

Governance latency is the time between a rule being broken and the organization finding out. Most enterprises already have the logs, the policies and the approval records. They just live in six different systems that only meet during an audit, usually via a frantically assembled spreadsheet.

Shorter latencies show up in the numbers a CFO already tracks: issues resolved sooner, less spent on each decision, fewer avoidable losses. The goal is to eliminate the wait, not the judgment.

Will you really have hundreds of agents?

A word on agents. An AI agent is software that can act on its own rather than only answer questions. In this series, agent always means an AI agent, and people are called by their roles.

Back to that storm. Does any single process need hundreds of agents? No. Rebooking one passenger needs one agent, maybe a few. So when do you need hundreds? In two situations:

  • Breadth: an agent or two for every employee (and eventually more), which means your employees' agents will soon be ignoring each other's emails on their behalf.
  • Depth: one part of the business, such as disruption recovery or claims, with hundreds of agents working at once, rebooking passengers into the same limited seats.

Depth is where the consequential cases are today, so that is where this series starts.

One storm, one airline, 470 AI agents

A thunderstorm brings a 90-minute ground stop at an airline's main hub, disrupting 300 flights and 48,500 passengers. At the peak, 470 AI agents are running, doing 14 different jobs. That doesn't mean 470 agents all talking at once. It works like the airport on a bad day: small teams, one for each open case (a disrupted flight, a stranded group, a bag that must follow its passenger), all reading the same departures board and competing for the same seats, crews and hotel rooms.

In this scenario, a group of 14 passengers misses its connection, and two agents reach for the last seats at the same time. The reservation system tells one of them "no," which is a setback for the agent but exactly what the architecture is supposed to do. When the ground stop lifts, agents build a recovery plan for 40 stranded flights, but nothing is final until a duty manager approves it. Nobody watched all 470 agents, and at that scale nobody could. The controls worked anyway.

Most decisions should be handled by rules or models, and only the hard ones should reach an AI agent.

Four questions before you delegate a decision

  1. Is it based on facts that are current enough? Not last night's report. Not what the agent happened to fetch a minute before another agent changed it.
  2. Is it made by the right decider? A rule, a model, an agent or a person, chosen on cost, risk and speed rather than on whichever one looked best in a demo.
  3. Can the AI act only within limits you set? Limits enforced by software when the action runs, rather than instructions in a prompt.
  4. Can you show who decided, why, under what authority and with what result? Months later, to someone who was not in the room and is not inclined to take your word for it.

If the honest answer to any of these is "we think so," you have found your first project. Answering them with confidence is what I call decision engineering: routing current facts to the right decider, checking every action against its limits before it happens and recording what was decided and what followed.

A decider is whatever makes the call: a rule, a predictive model, an AI agent or a person.

What makes a decision trustworthy

You can trust a decision when you can answer six questions about it:

  1. Who made it?
  2. Did the decider declare its intent before acting?
  3. Can you replay it from the logs later and, given the same inputs, get the same answer?
  4. Did it stay inside its guardrails?
  5. If it goes sideways, can you undo it (or at least clean up the mess)?
  6. Was it a good decision? Number six is the one everyone forgets. A decision can be sub-second, 100% policy-compliant, immutably audited and still completely wrong.

What this is not

Decision engineering is not for every decision: one low-risk decision living happily inside a well-run application should be left alone. It is not a product you buy off the shelf. Confluent, now part of IBM, provides the real-time foundation, and I am not going to pretend to be neutral about that, but the hard work is connecting what you already own.

How far to let AI go

Borrowing from the car industry's 0 to 5 scale for self-driving cars, here is a way to set how far AI can go. The car industry learned that the risky moment is the handover between machine and person. The handover is exactly where the controls should sit. In the storm, holding a flight for connecting passengers runs at level 4, rebooking a missed connection at level 3, and canceling a flight stays at level 2: the agents propose, a person decides.

LevelWhat happens
0 · ManualPeople decide and act.
1 · AssistedAI supplies context and predictions; people decide.
2 · RecommendAI proposes; a person approves each decision.
3 · SupervisedAI acts on routine cases within limits; exceptions go to people.
4 · BoundedAI acts across the process within enforced limits; people set policy and handle escalations.
5 · FullAI acts in all conditions with no person involved.

Most operations centers run at level 1 today. For consequential decisions, level 5 may not be the goal, and a decision moves up a level only on evidence.

What you can realistically achieve in 90 days

Start small. Pick one decision, make it trusted from end to end, and measure what changes. Ninety days is realistic for that, assuming the data, system access and a business owner are already in place. If any of those are missing, you will surface the gap in week one instead of week 10.

  1. Record a baselineMeasure how the decision is made today, so you can compare.
  2. Test alongside the old wayTest the new way of deciding alongside the old one, with only the old one acting.
  3. Act within tight limitsOnce it proves itself, let it act within tight limits.
  4. Pass the control testsBefore it gets more authority, it has to pass control tests that break things on purpose: stale data, two agents booking the same seat, a system failing halfway through a transaction.

That gives you real evidence before you scale it. To get the conversation started with your business, all you need is four things: the decision, its owner, the systems it touches and the measure the business will judge it by. If your four things look different from mine, I would like to hear why: find me on LinkedIn.

Where to go next

  • Post 2, Architecting for scale: what breaks between one agent and hundreds.
  • Post 3, Weathering the storm: what 470 AI agents do for one airline during one major thunderstorm.
  • Post 4, Working the cases: a group of 14 passengers and the hub restart, step by step.
  • Posts 5 to 8: for your architects. How context, deciders and routing fit together, how every action is checked before it lands, how to prove each decision can be trusted and how decision records are kept.

The full argument

Post 1 goes deeper into the full business case. It explains the two delays that slow AI down: how long it takes from something happening to the action being confirmed, and how long it takes to find out a rule was broken. It also covers the four things an enterprise needs in place before it hands decisions to AI, and why this wave of AI needs a discipline of its own.

Decision engineering · Post 1 of 9

Delegating decisions: why AI needs real-time, trusted decisions to act

Decision engineering for the agentic enterprise

Enterprise AI is moving beyond answers and recommendations. AI systems are starting to take part in business processes, making decisions and initiating actions in the systems that move money and goods. That creates a new requirement: an enterprise must be able to show that each of these decisions used current information, followed business policy, was carried out safely and left reliable evidence of what happened. Agent frameworks, data platforms and governance tools each solve a piece of the puzzle, and none of them talk to each other out of the box. Getting an AI agent to make a good decision is hard; making sure hundreds of independent decisions lead to actions the business can control, trust and account for is harder. Wiring those tools into a single, working architecture is what I call decision engineering: building systems where AI-driven decisions are fast, bounded, measurable and provable.

Daniel ShereckOctober 2026
00Summary

The argument in brief

  1. AI is moving from generating answers to making business decisions and initiating actions. The potential benefits are faster decisions, more work completed without manual intervention and a lower cost for each decision.
  2. You can only delegate a high-stakes decision when four things are true: it runs on live facts; it routes to the right decider; it passes hard software checks before acting; and it leaves behind enough evidence to prove it actually worked.
  3. In the airport thunderstorm example, rules take 80% of the decision evaluations and agents only 4.5%, yet agents carry about 40% of the money at stake. The numbers are illustrative, but the point holds: routing each decision to the right kind of decider is where the economic case starts. Measuring the cost, quality and outcome of each decision shows whether it's paying off.
  4. My reading of the last three years is that each wave of generative AI needed a new engineering practice before its results could be relied on. This wave needs one as well, and I call it decision engineering. It provides the mechanisms by which decisions are controlled, recorded and assessed, so that trust in them is justified.
  5. At the center is an append-only event log, which serves as the backbone of the architecture. Every rule, model and agent reads its context from the log and writes its decisions and outcomes back to it. It is the foundation of the architecture, though not the whole of it. Trust also requires controls that are enforced before an action takes effect, and audit controls that preserve the evidence and protect it from alteration.
  6. Put simply: every consequential business decision should have one verifiable record that connects its context, its authority, its execution and its outcome, whether a person, a rule, a model or an AI agent made it. Everything else in this series exists to produce that record.
  7. The technology exists today, with Confluent, now part of IBM, providing the real-time foundation. What most enterprises lack is the engineering practice that connects it to their decisions, their agents and the systems that hold their business records.
A decider is whatever makes the call: a rule, a predictive model, an AI agent or a person.
01The problem

From answers to actions

Automated decisions are not new. Credit scoring, fraud detection and industrial control have relied on them for decades, each built for one narrow, well-structured decision. Generative AI makes decisions differently from the automation that came before it. It first came into wide use helping people find information, write content and complete tasks, with a person reading every answer. Now enterprises are moving it into the role the older systems held, across a far wider range of decisions, including ones that depend on unstructured information and span several systems. There, AI recommends and initiates actions that have financial, operational and customer consequences: rebooking a passenger, releasing a payment, reordering stock or dispatching a crew.

A chief information officer or chief AI officer therefore faces a practical question: how can the enterprise safely let AI make more consequential decisions, using the systems and data it already has? A wrong answer in a chat window is easy to spot and discard. A bad call in SAP or a reservation system moves real money or strands a customer before anyone knows it happened.

Two measures of delay describe the problem. Decision latency is the time between something happening in the business and someone or something acting on it. It is measured to the point at which the action is confirmed in the system of record, because a fast recommendation does not help if the action that follows it is slow. A complex insurance claim can take days or weeks, and a commercial credit decision can pass through several reviews, systems and teams. This delay often has no single owner and never appears as a line in a budget, yet its cost shows up everywhere: in lost sales, write-offs and the staff whose job is to move cases along a queue.

Governance latency is the time between a control being violated and the organization knowing about it. Closing that gap takes monitoring; explaining the violation afterwards takes records that show which data, permissions and policies applied to that single decision. Most enterprises already have those records, just scattered across different systems. AI that cannot explain its decisions rarely makes it past a pilot. Governance is what gets an AI system into production, which is why governance latency belongs alongside decision latency as a standard measure.

Delegating a high-stakes decision requires four capabilities:

CapabilityBusiness questionBusiness value
Real-time contextIs the decision based on information that is current and consistent?Fewer wrong decisions caused by stale or conflicting data
DecisionsIs each decision made by the right decider, whether a rule, a model, an agent or a person?Faster processing and a lower cost for each decision
Controlled actionsCan AI act only within defined business and security limits?Lower operational risk, and more work that can be automated safely
TrustCan the enterprise show who decided, why, under what authority and with what result?Accountability, compliance and the confidence to extend autonomy further

Posts 5 to 7 describe these capabilities in detail. The problem they address does not depend on having many agents; it arises whenever several independent actors, human or automated, can affect the same business process while working from overlapping information and holding different levels of authority. Even hundreds of agents rarely work together on one decision. What they do is make many different decisions that affect the same operation and compete for the same resources, as the next post will show.

Not every decision needs all four capabilities. A single low-risk decision inside a well-run application is fine with that application's own logic, transactions and audit log. These capabilities earn their keep when facts change across several systems, multiple actors are involved, processes run for hours or days or a wrong action has real consequences.

02The arc

From prompts to decisions

The engineering focus of generative AI has moved quickly since 2023, and I break it into five stages. Each year the amount of work an AI system can do unsupervised has grown, and each increase has needed a new engineering discipline before the result could be relied on.

The five stagesA deeper definition of each stage
  • Prompt engineering is the craft of wording an instruction so that a language model gives a useful answer.
  • Retrieval engineering adds an organization's own documents and data to the prompt, a technique known as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), so that the answer rests on facts the model was not trained on.
  • Context engineering manages everything the model sees at each step of a longer task, including its instructions, its memory of earlier steps and the results of the tools it has called.
  • Harness engineering builds the environment around the model: the tools it may use, the tests that check its work, the permissions that limit it and the feedback that lets it correct itself. An agent is commonly described as a model plus a harness. Anthropic now says the same about safety: a well-trained model can still be exploited through a poorly configured harness or an overly permissive tool.[49] Research systems can now refine a harness automatically, from its prompt and guardrails to its tools and skills, while the model stays the same.[18] The harness may be synthesized or evolved by the system itself; the controls around it may not, which is the boundary between harness engineering and what this series describes.
  • Decision engineering, the subject of this series, designs, routes, controls and records the decisions that AI makes or assists, so that each one can be trusted. A trusted decision is attributable, explainable, reconstructable, bounded, reversible where possible and evaluated for quality. Post 7 defines each of these terms.

In practice the stages overlap, but the terms are in wide use. OpenAI gave harness engineering currency in February 2026 with an account of how its own teams build the scaffolding and controls around coding agents.[12] Prompt, context and harness engineering are now described as successive phases of one maturity curve.[13] The fifth stage doesn't have an industry buzzword yet, so I'm staking a claim on decision engineering. Gartner already defines decision intelligence as engineering how decisions are made.[41] I use decision engineering for the runtime layer beneath that, which nobody has yet pulled together end to end: the records, the controls, the latency and the cost per decision, and what happens when rules, predictive models, AI agents and humans have to make calls together in real time. I use the term process agent for an agent that takes part in a business process as a full actor, working with other agents and with people over hours or days.

Why coding agents came first

Coding agents became useful before other kinds of agents because software development already had a harness. They still produce faulty changes, but the means of catching and reversing those changes were already in place. A compiler rejects malformed code, a test suite catches many errors and gives evidence that the work is correct, and version control records every change and its author. A sandbox limits the damage a mistake can cause, and a single command can revert a bad code change. But the effects a change has already had in production, such as altered data or completed transactions, often cannot be reverted the same way. Harness engineering largely consisted of connecting agents to machinery that software teams had built over several decades. Anthropic's auto mode for its Claude Code agent makes the point directly: file edits inside a project run without a check because version control can undo them, while shell commands, web requests and calls to outside tools go to a separate classifier first.[48]

You can't run git revert on a wired payment, and there is no compiler for a rebooked family of four. Decision engineering is the work of building that missing safety net for the rest of the business:

What a coding agent already hasWhat it providesWhat must be built for a process agent
Version controlA record of every change, in order, with its authorAn event log that records every signal, decision and action, each tied to the identity of the agent responsible
Test suiteEvidence that work is correct before it is releasedThe ability to re-run recorded events through a decision and compare the results, both before a change goes live and after the fact
Compiler and type checkerRejection of malformed workSchemas, which define the structure every event must have, enforced at the point where events are written
SandboxA limit on what a mistake can affectLimits on what each agent may spend, change and call
Code reviewApproval by a second party before a change is mergedReview of an agent's plan before it takes a consequential action
RevertA way to undo a changeA classification of every action as reversible, compensable (offset by a later action, such as a refund) or irreversible, with tested compensating actions and stricter approval for actions that cannot be undone

A harness keeps one agent from going off the rails. Decision engineering keeps 470 of them from creating a financial or operational incident at scale.

03The value

Measuring the value

Automating a bad decision just lets you lose money at machine speed. If your automation rate goes up alongside refunds, rework and compliance fines, you haven't improved the business, which is why these metrics have to be read as a set.

What is measuredMeasure
Faster responseDecision latency: the time from a business event to a confirmed action, with detection, decision, authorization and execution timed separately
Faster detection of control failuresGovernance latency: the time from a control being violated to the organization knowing
More automationShare of decisions resolved without manual intervention
Lower costCost of each completed decision or case
Better outcomes for customersA measure specific to the process, such as the share of passengers rebooked successfully or missed connections avoided
Lower riskNumber of duplicate, unauthorized or non-compliant actions prevented before they took effect
Better auditabilityShare of decisions with complete evidence that can be verified independently, and the time needed to investigate one decision
Total costThe full cost of the solution, including streaming, models, agents, integration, governance and human oversight

This series does not offer return-on-investment figures, because they depend on the process and the starting point. An enterprise should record a baseline for each measure on the decision it selects, before any change is made, and compare the same measures afterwards. The 90-day plan in post 9 builds this in.

Decision engineering · Post 2 of 9

Architecting for scale: what breaks between one agent and hundreds

One agent can be watched by the team that built it. Four hundred cannot. Here is where those agents come from, what breaks when they share a live operation and the five architectural problems you have to solve next.

03The fleet

From one agent to hundreds

As enterprises introduce agents into more processes, the number operating at the same time grows by orders of magnitude, and each step changes how they must be managed. This series is about the step to hundreds of agents.

A reader may reasonably ask whether hundreds of agents would ever work together, and for a single process that skepticism is justified. Rebooking one passenger or settling one claim needs a handful of agents at most, often just one. Most of the decisions in it should go to a rule or a small model, which can make them in milliseconds at a fraction of the cost, as post 5 explains. Even so, there are two situations in which a company finds itself running hundreds of agents.

The first is breadth. Suppose every employee ends up with one or two agents that act for them, and those agents coordinate with each other. A company with tens of thousands of employees then has tens of thousands of agents. Some of the most visible agents today write and review code, and the next step is to arrange meetings, prepare handoffs and request approvals on behalf of their owners.

The second is depth. One value stream, meaning one domain of the business such as disruption recovery at an airline or claims at an insurer, could have hundreds of agents working in it at the same time. Each agent would have a narrow job, and all of them would draw on the same facts and compete for the same resources. The agents commit the company's money and capacity, and a mistake by one of them can affect the others within seconds.

A value stream behaves differently from a single process: dozens of processes run in parallel, each with its own agents, all acting on the same live operation. Four factors multiply the agent count:

What multipliesWhy separate agents are neededExamples
CasesA case is one piece of work that stays open until it is resolved, such as a disrupted flight or a disputed claim. Difficult cases run for hours or days, and each one has its own state, history and open questions. One agent per open case is the natural unit.An agent for every disrupted flight, every disputed claim or every delayed shipment
External partiesPartners and suppliers are showing up with their own agents, and customers aren't far behind. You did not build them, you do not control their prompts and you cannot treat them as trusted.A partner airline's agent, a supplier's scheduling agent, a customer's personal agent
ChecksWork that matters is reviewed by a second agent that has a different owner, a different model or a different mandate.Agents that review plans, check policy compliance or settle disagreements between other agents
Processes that share a subjectThe same customer is handled by sales, service, billing, fraud and finance. Each process has its own agents, and all of them must work from the same facts.Thirty processes reading and writing events about one customer

The result looks like an org chart: dozens of small, specialized teams working from the same facts. That means you can't govern this by inspecting one agent's chat log; you have to govern the system as a whole.

04At scale

What breaks at hundreds of agents

In most pilots, agents call each other point-to-point, share a couple of over-privileged API keys and rely on a developer squinting at trace logs when things break. Good architects know better, but pilot code has a habit of becoming production code, and point-to-point falls apart the moment you scale from 10 agents to 100.

ConcernWith 10 agentsWith 470 agentsWhat is required
Working togetherAgents call each other directly.Up to 110,215 direct links are possible. Only some of them will exist, but one slow agent still delays every agent that calls it, and nobody knows which agents depend on which.Communication through topics, so that agents are decoupled and a slow subscriber delays mainly itself, although shared downstream resources can still be a bottleneck
Shared factsEach agent queries the source system when it needs data.Two agents read the same record a few seconds apart and reach opposite conclusions.Context (the facts a decider reads before it decides) served from the log and read as of one stated point in time
Conflicting commitmentsConflicts are rare enough to correct by hand.Two agents see the last seat on a flight and both promise it. Shared context does not prevent this, because each agent acts before it can see the other's booking.Commitments made through the action gateway, described in post 6, as conditional updates, so that the second booking is refused
Calling toolsAPI keys are kept in a configuration file.With 470 agents and 20 systems there are 9,400 possible grants, and nobody can say which agents are able to issue compensation.One gateway policy enforced beside each system, not through one central proxy that every call must pass through; short-lived credentials tied to each agent's identity; and rate budgets per agent and tool, so one runaway agent can't starve the rest
LoopsThe team notices and intervenes.Agents trigger other agents. An agent or stream job reacts to an event that its own earlier output caused, and the activity feeds itself.A record on every event of what caused it, a limit on the length of any causal chain (a sequence of events in which each one causes the next), and budgets that stop a runaway agent
FailureThe agent is restarted.Half-finished work piles up across the fleet, and a naive retry hands the same stranded passenger two hotel vouchers.Actions that are safe to repeat, a compensating action wherever one exists, and state that survives a restart
OversightSomeone reads the traces.There are 200,000 decision evaluations in six hours, which is more than any team can read.A structured record of every decision, queues for exceptions, review of a sample and replay
LifecycleThe team knows each agent by name.Unmanaged agents accumulate: some have no owner, some run on six-month-old prompts and the person who built them has moved to another department.A registry that gives each agent an accountable owner, an expiry date and periodic recertification

Reliability does not compose

A harness can make each step reliable, but a business process chains many steps across many agents, and the odds multiply. The table assumes failures are independent and nothing recovers. That's a simplification, but the direction holds.

Steps in the chainEach step 99%, raised to the number of stepsChance that every step succeeds
100.991090.4%
200.992081.8%
500.995060.5%

Trying to polish every step from 99% to 99.9% reliability is a great way to burn your AI budget without ever reaching certainty. Distributed systems engineers learned to design for this decades ago: assume steps will fail, make every action safe to repeat, and plan in advance how each completed action will be reversed or compensated. That is a property of the architecture, and no amount of work on one agent's prompt or harness will produce it. Improving individual agents is not enough; the whole workflow needs explicit failure and recovery behavior.

Five underlying problems

  • Time. Agents reason over snapshots of data. Every decision is valid only for a limited period, and its inputs must be consistent as of the moment of the decision. Data from last night's load does not meet that standard.
  • Coordination. Agents now produce enterprise events as well as consume them. The event streaming you built for applications becomes the coordination channel for your agents.
  • Implicit decisions. Right now, most AI decisions are buried inside a 2,000-word prompt and an opaque model call. They have no schema, no version and no owner, which makes them impossible to reproduce six months later.
  • Side effects. Actions change systems of record. A fabricated sentence in a chat response is embarrassing, whereas a duplicated payment is a financial loss.
  • Evidence. Traces are diagnostic telemetry: often sampled, held by the team that produced them and collected after the event. An auditor, a regulator or a court requires independently verifiable evidence that is complete and preserved for the required retention period, which is a different thing.

The way out: a shared log

The alternative to direct calls is for agents to communicate through the event log. An agent publishes events to a named stream, called a topic, and other agents subscribe to the topics that are relevant to their work. The publisher does not need to know who is listening. Figure 2.3 compares the two approaches.

Put together, the parts form one architecture. Figure 2.4 is the map for the rest of the series: posts 3 and 4 run a storm across it, posts 5 to 7 build one part each, and post 8 shows it in full detail. Select any part to see what it does and where the series covers it.

Decision engineering · Post 3 of 9

Weathering the storm: what 470 AI agents do for one airline

This post follows the 14 kinds of agent that recover one airline's operation after a storm, and the controls that keep them in line.

05The storm

A worked example: an airline's digital twin during a storm

One example runs from here to the end of the series. A large airline is building a digital twin of its operation: a live software model of every aircraft, crew, gate, bag and passenger, kept current by a continuous flow of events from the systems and equipment that handle them. Airlines already use models of this kind to simulate their operation, for example to test a schedule before it is published. This airline wants to go further, from simulating the operation to making decisions within it.

The twin's hardest test is a disruption. On a summer afternoon, a line of thunderstorms brings a ground stop at the airline's main hub: for 90 minutes no departures leave, and lightning suspends work on the ramp. The disruption hits 300 flights and 48,500 passengers. This series follows the first six hours of recovery decisions; the effects on crews, aircraft and passengers can run well into the next day. The airport runs an integrated operations center of its own, where security, emergency dispatch, facilities and airline liaisons share one live view of the airfield, gates, checkpoint queues, roadways and parking. The airline's agents work with it as a separate organization with its own authority. Disruption recovery is the value stream, the domain of the business, that this example follows. The figures are illustrative, chosen so that the arithmetic is easy to follow.

In this situation, minutes matter. Crew members may work only a limited number of hours, called their duty limit, so a crew that is legal to fly at 3:10 p.m. may not be at 3:40 p.m. A connecting passenger can be saved by holding a departure for eight minutes, but only if the decision is made before the aircraft door closes. Each delayed flight also delays the next flight that uses the same aircraft, crew or gate.

A decision evaluation is one application of a decision to one flight or passenger. Each disrupted flight requires about 20 of them, such as whether to delay, cancel or divert it, which aircraft and crew to assign and which gate to use. Each passenger requires about four, such as whether to rebook, whether a connection is at risk, where to send baggage and what compensation is due. That amounts to 6,000 flight evaluations and 194,000 passenger evaluations, or 200,000 decision evaluations in six hours. The count treats every evaluation separately. Some are settled together, as when one decision to hold a departure covers all of its connecting passengers, so the number of distinct decisions is lower. Most are routine, and rules and solvers settle them. (To keep the taxonomy clean, I group solvers in the "model" tier, leaving four deciders: rules, models, agents and people.) About 9,000 evaluations reach an agent because the rules and solvers cannot settle them, and these belong to cases that stay open for an hour or more. A case is one piece of work that stays open until it is resolved, such as a disrupted flight or a group booking.

Counting the agents

Here, as throughout the series, an agent is always an AI agent; the airline's people are named by their roles: duty managers, gate staff, crew schedulers and contact-center staff. Counting agents takes two terms, much like classes and objects in code. An agent definition is the template: the role, its instructions and the tools it may use. An agent instance is one running copy of that template, working on one case or watching one entity, such as an aircraft or a crew. Each instance has its own authenticated identity and is given authority only for the case it is working on, so two itinerary agents cannot see each other's passengers. Authority also governs what an agent may read. Shared operational facts, such as gate availability and crew positions, are published to every agent, while passenger and case information is released only through a service that checks the agent's authority for that case before returning anything. At the peak of the disruption, the airline is running 470 agent instances created from 14 agent definitions. Figure 3.2 groups the 470 instances into four families, and the table that follows it names each definition.

These numbers are small beside 300 flights and 48,500 passengers because rules, models and solvers handle most of the work. The 9,000 difficult evaluations belong to about 1,800 cases: a flight with no legal crew, a group booking no single flight can carry, a bag that must follow a rebooked passenger, a disputed expense claim. Each case involves about five evaluations by agents on average, often by the same agent, and stays open for about an hour, which puts about 300 cases open at once on average over the six hours.

At the peak, about 400 cases are open. Most agents work on one case, but some, like maintenance and recovery coordination, work across many, so 420 agents run inside the airline's operation. Another 50 airline-owned liaison agents deal with partners, the airport and suppliers, for 470. The partners' own agents aren't counted.

Treat these numbers as illustrative, not as a capacity-planning guide. An agent instance is not a continuously running model consuming GPU time; it is a lightweight state machine that owns one case and stays idle between Kafka events. One instance per case gives each case its own state, authority and accountability.

Here is the full roster of 14 agent definitions at the peak of the storm:

Agent definitionWhat it decides during the stormWorks withInstances at peak
Flight recovery agentRecovers one disrupted flight that the solvers cannot resolve. It proposes a new departure time, aircraft and crew, or a cancellation.Crew recovery, maintenance, and gate and turnaround agents40
Crew recovery agentFinds a legal crew for a flight whose crew is out of duty hours or out of position, and arranges the crew's hotel and transport.Flight recovery and partner liaison agents30
Gate and turnaround agentReassigns gates and reorders the fueling, catering and cleaning of an aircraft when the plan changes.Airport and supplier liaison agents30
Maintenance agentChecks each proposed aircraft swap against the checks that are due and the defects that are open. It can refuse a swap.Flight recovery agents, engineers10
Recovery coordination agentCombines the proposals of the other flight operations agents into one recovery plan for a bank of departures, a wave of flights that leave close together so that passengers can connect, and finds the conflicts between them.All flight operations agents, duty managers5
Itinerary agentRebooks one complex itinerary, such as a group, a journey on several airlines or a missed long-haul connection.Flight recovery, baggage and partner liaison agents150
Customer communication agentAnswers passengers in the app and the contact center, and tells them only what has been committed.Itinerary, baggage and compensation agents40
Compensation agentDecides the vouchers, refunds and expense claims that the rules and the models cannot settle, under applicable law and airline policy.Itinerary agents, finance systems30
Special assistance agentArranges care for unaccompanied children, wheelchair users and passengers with medical needs.Itinerary and airport liaison agents15

All 14 definitions470

Most collaboration in this picture is small. Finding new flights for a group that has missed its connection involves an itinerary agent, a flight recovery agent, a baggage agent and perhaps the agents of a partner airline and a hotel. More than a hundred such collaborations are running at the same time. All of them read the same weather findings, the same gate availability and the same crew positions, and all of them can request commitments of the airline's seats, hotel rooms and money, each within its own scope and limits. The agents work in small teams, one team for each case, and most agents never exchange a message with an agent on another case. The teams meet through the resources they share and the facts they all read.

The one large collaboration is the recovery of the hub itself, where more than 100 agents contribute proposals and checks to a single plan that a person approves; the second case below describes it. The difficulty at this scale is that hundreds of agents are making different decisions that affect the same operation and compete for the same limited resources.

Where the decisions are made

The twin also shows where decisions are made and who should make each of them. Figure 3.3 shows a single aircraft at its gate, together with the locations where data originates, the parties involved at each location and the kind of decider that works there. Rules, models, solvers and people take most of the decision evaluations at most locations. Agents work at every location except the weather feed, and they handle the cases that need reasoning or that involve another party. The agent counts in the figure are for the whole hub and not for this one aircraft.

What this post established. The 470 are peak concurrent instances of 14 agent definitions, not 14 agents and not 470 kinds of work. Almost all of them work on one case each, a few watch shared resources or combine proposals, and most decisions never reach them at all: rules, models and solvers take the routine share, and the agents take the few cases that carry most of the money at stake.
