Decision engineering · Post 4 of 9

Working the cases: a group of 14 passengers and the hub restart, step by step

Post 3 counted the agents. This post follows them through two cases: a group of 14 passengers who miss their connection, and the restart of the hub, where more than 100 agents contribute to a single plan. Then the same pattern in insurance.

05The cases

Two cases from the storm

A case of moderate complexity: a group of 14 passengers

Two cases from the storm show how the parts fit together. The first is of moderate complexity and involves six agents. A group of 14 passengers traveling together on one booking misses its connection. The rules cannot rebook them, because no single flight tonight has 14 free seats, so the group must be split or moved to the morning, and the case goes to an itinerary agent. Each step below names the control that applies, figure 2.4 shows where each one sits, and posts 5 to 8 explain each control. Figure 4.1 then shows the same nine steps as a process diagram, with one row for each participant.

  1. An agent takes the caseAn itinerary agent is started for this booking. It has its own identity, and its authority covers these 14 passengers and nobody else.
    Delegated authority
  2. It learns from another agentThe best option tonight splits the group across two flights, but the second flight has no legal crew. The flight recovery agent handling that flight publishes its finding that the second flight will be canceled, and the itinerary agent reads it from the shared event log, the record of events that every agent reads, without calling the other agent.
    Shared context
  3. Two agents want the same seatsThe agent tries to book the last seats on the first flight tomorrow. Another itinerary agent tries at the same moment. The reservation system accepts the first booking and refuses the second, so the seats are not promised twice.
    Conditional commitment
  4. A partner's agent is involvedA partner liaison agent asks a partner airline's AI agent for 14 seats. That agent belongs to another company, so its identity and its offer are verified before the airline relies on either.
    Trust between organizations
  5. A prompt injection falls flatThe partner's reply contains an embedded instruction telling the reader to waive all booking fees. The agent treats the reply as untrusted data, but that alone guarantees nothing. What stops the waiver is the gateway's fee policy, a deterministic check: waiving fees needs a duty manager's approval, and no wording in a message can grant it. An action that is authorized but still unwise is what the plan review and guardians are for.
    Untrusted content
  6. The plan is reviewedThe agent proposes seats on the partner's morning flight, seven hotel rooms and vouchers for 14 people. Rules check the plan against policy, and a duty manager approves it because the total is above the agent's limit.
    Plan review and limits
  7. The policy changes meanwhileWhile the plan waits for approval, operations control issues a new version of the voucher policy. The action gateway, which post 6 describes, checks the action against the version in force at the moment it is committed.
    Authority rechecked
  8. The actions are confirmedSeats, rooms and vouchers are committed and then confirmed against the reservation and finance systems, a check called reconciliation. The partner's systems accept the reissued tickets and the bag transfer under the two airlines' interline agreement, which lets each airline rebook the other's passengers, tickets and bags. One hotel booking times out and is retried safely without double-booking a room, and a baggage agent reads the confirmed itinerary from the log to reroute the group's 14 bags.
    Safe repetition and reconciliation
  9. The case can be rebuiltMonths later, the airline can show each decision, the agent that made it, the policy version that applied and the outcome the systems of record confirmed.
    Decision evidence

This one case involved six agents: two itinerary agents competing for the same seats, a flight recovery agent, a partner liaison agent, a baggage agent and an agent that belongs to a partner. About 150 itinerary agents are running at the peak of the storm, each on one case. No person can watch each of them, so the controls have to work on their own.

A complex case: restarting the hub

The second case is the largest in the storm, and it starts before the ground stop. About two hours ahead, the airport's disruption forecast shows a high likelihood that departures will be cut, and the airline's observers, small monitoring jobs that watch the event stream and flag what matters, publish it as a finding on the log. Crew recovery agents begin positioning reserve crews, and partner liaison agents place provisional holds on hotel blocks, all within their limits and released if the storm misses. When the ground stop lifts after 90 minutes, the airport can handle only half its usual number of departures for the next two hours. The solvers produce a recovery plan for most of the 300 disrupted flights. Forty flights remain that the solvers cannot resolve, because each one lacks a legal crew, a serviceable aircraft, a gate or a departure slot. These 40 flights compete with each other for the same scarce resources, so they cannot be recovered one at a time.

  1. One agent takes each flightA flight recovery agent is started for each of the 40 flights. Each agent has authority over its own flight and over nothing else.
    Delegated authority
  2. The agents use solvers as toolsEach agent asks the solver and the delay models for options, then publishes a proposal: a departure time with an aircraft, a crew and a gate, or a cancellation. Each proposal is a decision record: a record of what was decided, by which decider and on which facts.
    Decision records
  3. The proposals conflictThirty-six proposals ask to depart in the first hour, which has 24 free slots, and nine ask for the same four spare aircraft. Five recovery coordination agents, one for each bank of departures, read the proposals from the log and identify every conflict.
    Shared context
  4. Crew limits set the orderThirty crew recovery agents work on the crews. One of them reports that the crew of a long-haul flight will pass its duty limit in 50 minutes. The coordination agents move that flight forward, and a short-haul flight whose crew has hours to spare takes a later slot.
    Shared context
  5. A swap is refusedA flight recovery agent proposes to use a spare aircraft. A maintenance agent finds that the aircraft has a check due before the flight would land, and it refuses the swap. The flight recovery agent has no authority to overrule the refusal, so it proposes a different aircraft.
    Separation of duties
  6. Each resource is claimed onceEvery aircraft, crew and hotel block the airline controls is held through the action gateway on the condition that it is still free. Gates and departure slots are not the airline's to hold: they are requested from the airport and air traffic control, which allocate them. A hold is provisional: it expires or is released if the plan is not approved, and it becomes a commitment only when the plan is. When two agents try to hold the same aircraft, one succeeds and the other agent is told immediately, so no resource appears twice in the plan.
    Conditional commitment
  7. The airport and suppliers agreeAirport liaison agents request gates from the airport's agent and, through the airline's usual coordination channels, propose departure times within the flow restrictions air traffic control has set (air traffic control, of course, still issues every clearance). Meanwhile, supplier liaison agents agree on new fueling and catering times with the ground handlers' agents. Every external reply is verified before the plan relies on it.
    Trust between organizations
  8. A person approves the planThe combined plan sends 31 flights, reschedules 3 to later departure slots and cancels 6. A cancellation exceeds the authority of any agent, so the plan goes to the duty manager, who approves it as a whole. That approval covers the airline's commercial choices; dispatchers, pilots, maintenance and air traffic control keep their own authority, and every departure still needs its air traffic control clearance.
    Plan review and limits
  9. The rest of the operation followsThe approved plan is published to the log. Itinerary agents rebook the passengers on canceled flights, baggage and cargo agents redirect bags and shipments, and gate and turnaround agents reorder the ground work. Customer communication agents tell passengers only what has been committed, and because the airport forecasts long checkpoint queues for the first morning wave, they stagger the recommended arrival times in the rebooking notices.
    Shared context
  10. One agent gets stuck in a loopA flight recovery agent begins flooding the slot-coordination channel with the same request five times a second. Stream monitoring spots the spike, revokes the agent's credentials in seconds, reconciles its unfinished holds so nothing is left dangling and hands the flight to a fresh instance.
    Monitoring and revocation
  11. The weather changes the planA second storm cell closes one runway for 20 minutes. Operations control lowers the limit on departures, and the new policy version reaches every decider. Actions that are not yet committed are rechecked and stopped. Four committed departures are given later slots, and hotel rooms that are no longer needed are released.
    Authority rechecked, compensation
  12. The evening is replayedA week later, the airline replays the evening with a different rule for crews close to their duty limit, and compares the two outcomes before it changes the policy.
    Replay and what-if

About 145 instances contributed proposals and checks to this plan: the 115 flight operations agents and the 30 airport and supplier liaison agents. The other 325, mainly the passenger, baggage, cargo and partner liaison agents, carried it out case by case. No agent called another of the airline's agents directly. They published proposals, read each other's findings and claimed shared resources through the gateway, and a person approved the plan. Figure 4.2 shows this arrangement. Post 2 described what goes wrong when the same work is attempted without these shared mechanisms; posts 5 to 8 show how each one is built.

Step 8 is the control everyone points to and the one I trust least. A duty manager approving a 40-flight plan mid-storm is reading the clock, not the plan. So the review is built for a person with four minutes: the six cancellations, the conflicts the agents could not settle, the deviations from policy and the money committed, with the routine departures summarized. And the override rate is watched. If a manager has never changed a plan, the review has become a rubber stamp. The AI Act names the risk: Article 14 requires oversight designed against automation bias.[44]

The same pattern in insurance

The pattern applies in other industries. In insurance, the decision is whether to approve, hold or deny a claim, and it follows these steps.

  1. A claim is filed, and the first notice of loss, the initial report of the claim, arrives as an event. Policy data from the core system, which often runs on a mainframe and remains the system of record, is captured as events by change data capture, which copies each change in a database into the event stream.
  2. Stream processing validates the claim, removes duplicates, masks personal data and adds the policy and the claimant's history.
  3. A decision service, the software that applies the rules and models, reads the version of the policy that is in force and obtains a score from a model.
  4. The decision to approve, hold or deny is published with a record of the data, the policy version and the model version that produced it.
  5. The action gateway writes the decision into the claims system and requests the payment. A held claim is sent to an adjuster with the full record, and the adjuster's decision returns as an event.
  6. The lakehouse, a store that combines a data lake with analytics tools, receives every event and uses them to retrain the model and to review the policy.
  7. Months later, a question about why the claim was denied is answered from the decision record, together with the record of which policies and permissions were in force on that date. The record establishes what was decided and on what basis; whether the decision was fair or legally sufficient is a separate judgment that the evidence supports.

A card dispute at a bank follows the same steps with different sources and a different model. Posts 5 to 8 describe the mechanisms on which both examples rely.

When to add an agent. A separate agent is justified when the work has its own long-lived state, a different owner or level of authority, a different time scale or a need for an independent check. If none of these conditions applies, a rule, a model or a solver is the better decider, and a stream processing job is the better way to produce a signal. Agents belong on the exception path, and the number of agents grows because exceptions remain open for a long time.

What this post established. Two cases show the agents at work. Almost all of them work on one case each; a few watch shared resources or combine proposals, and a person approves the plan that commits the airline. What kept them in line was not the log on its own but the conditional hold at the system of record, the authority delegated for one case and the record left behind.

Next in the series

The storm shows several hundred agents working with shared mechanisms in place. The next post starts building them: real-time context that every decider can rely on, and decisions that are made explicit and routed to the right kind of decider.

Decision engineering · Post 5 of 9

Deciding in real time: how context, deciders and routing fit together

Posts 2 to 4 showed what breaks at hundreds of agents and what a storm demands of them. This post covers the first two of the four capabilities that fix it: real-time context and decisions.

06The framework

Real-time, decisions, actions and trust

The framework is a loop with three steps, together with one property that applies to all of them. An enterprise senses what is happening, decides what to do and acts on the decision, and the outcome informs the next round. Trust comes from three things working together on every turn of that loop: evidence that can be verified, controls enforced before an action takes effect, and measurement of whether the decisions were good.

The loop runs on the map in figure 2.4: sensing happens on the shared log, deciding in the deciders and acting through the gateway, with trust and learning underneath. This post and the next two build those parts one at a time.

The loop runs at two speeds. The decision loop acts in the moment, within milliseconds or minutes, on a streaming platform, which in this architecture is Confluent. The learning loop works over hours and days in a lakehouse (a store that combines a data lake with analytics tools) such as Databricks or Snowflake. It studies the recorded decisions and their outcomes, retrains models, reviews policies and sends the updated models and rules back to the decision loop, so that recorded outcomes become the evidence for improving the process.

Confluent is my choice, and I am not neutral about it. The architecture itself asks for less: an ordered, retained, replayable log with keys and schemas, and stateful stream processing over it. Any platform that provides those will do. A message queue that forgets each event once it is read will not, because replay and the governance log depend on the history staying put.

Real-time

Definition. Real-time means that each decision uses information that is recent enough for the action being considered, and that the decision takes effect while it still matters. A payment authorization may need an answer in milliseconds, while a decision to hold a departing flight may have several minutes. When a decision must be answered in milliseconds, every network hop (each call between systems) eats into the latency budget, the total delay allowed, so the gateway check runs in the same process or right beside the system of record. When important information is missing or too old, the system must know whether to wait, request an update, escalate the decision or decline to act.

What this requires
  • A freshness target for each type of decision, measured as the age of the context at decision time
  • Processing based on the time an event occurred, so that late and out-of-order events are handled correctly
  • A declared and validated view of the inputs to each decision as of a stated time, with known limits on the freshness and completeness of each source
  • History that is retained and can be replayed
  • Defined behavior when critical information is missing or too old: wait, request an update, escalate or decline to act
  • Data contracts, which specify the structure and quality rules for each type of event, enforced where events are written
What runs it
  • Confluent provides the event log (Apache Kafka), stream processing that keeps state between events (Apache Flink) and a schema registry, a shared catalog of event structures, with data contracts.
  • Confluent's Real-Time Context Engine serves current context to agents through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the emerging standard by which agents reach tools and data, using Confluent’s existing access controls. For passenger and case-specific information, an additional context service verifies each agent’s identity and delegated authority and enforces record-level access before returning it.[2]
  • Change data capture, which converts database changes into events, brings core systems onto the log.
  • A lakehouse such as Databricks or Snowflake holds long-term history.
Flink SQLBuilds the context under stated timing rules. Illustrative. 
-- Status updates for inbound flights, with the time each update was issued.
-- The watermark is a chosen lateness policy: events later than it are not waited for, and the application decides whether to drop or correct for them.
CREATE TABLE flight_status (
  flight_id STRING, hub STRING, crew_pairing_id STRING,
  delay_minutes INT, est_arrival TIMESTAMP_LTZ(3),
  event_time TIMESTAMP_LTZ(3),
  WATERMARK FOR event_time AS event_time - INTERVAL '5' SECOND
);

-- Signal: the number of delayed flights at each hub over a sliding 15 minutes
CREATE VIEW hub_pressure AS
SELECT hub, window_end, COUNT(DISTINCT flight_id) AS delayed_flights_15m
FROM TABLE(HOP(TABLE flight_status, DESCRIPTOR(event_time), INTERVAL '1' MINUTE, INTERVAL '15' MINUTES))
WHERE delay_minutes > 15
GROUP BY hub, window_start, window_end;

-- Temporal join: read the crew duty record that was in force at the moment
-- of each status update. crew_duty_versions is a versioned table.
INSERT INTO flight_context
SELECT s.flight_id, s.est_arrival, d.duty_ends_at,
       d.version AS duty_version, s.event_time AS context_as_of
FROM flight_status AS s
JOIN crew_duty_versions FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF s.event_time AS d
  ON s.crew_pairing_id = d.crew_pairing_id;

The final statement is the important detail. It is a temporal join: it combines each flight status event with the version of the crew duty record that was in force at the time of that event. The result is a consistent view of the flight status and crew duty information available under the stated timing and completeness rules. If an agent fetches those two facts via REST calls a minute apart, it might pair a fresh arrival time with a stale duty record and conclude that a crew is legal to fly when it is actually about to time out, and the agent's reasoning trace will still look completely logical.

This guarantee is limited by the quality of the sources. It depends on complete data, correct timestamps, the handling of late events and properly versioned tables. It cannot show that every change in the real world was captured or that every source is authoritative, which is why the requirements above include a defined response to missing or stale information. A consistent view as of an event time is also not a snapshot of every system at once, nor the current state of the authoritative systems. The design keeps four times separate: when an event occurred, when it was processed, when a fact or policy took effect and when the decision was made.

Observers produce the signals

Feeding raw event streams directly to an LLM agent is prohibitively expensive and unnecessary. Deciders need distilled signals, which is the job of observers: lightweight Flink jobs or small models that watch the raw stream and publish a finding only when something meaningful shifts. An observer needs a decision model or a language model only when its input is unstructured, such as free-text maintenance notes. For that reason they are not counted among the 470 agents. Each observer listens to a topic, filters and aggregates what it receives, and publishes a higher-level event when something meaningful emerges. An observer detects a condition; it is not the component authorized to act on it, and the decision and the action belong to the deciders and the gateway. Other observers consume those events and repeat the pattern, so that each layer detects more sophisticated conditions than the layer below it.

Decisions

Definition. A decision is an explicit, versioned object with defined inputs and outputs and a named owner, and a record is written every time it is made. Each decision is routed to the least expensive decider that is competent to make it, where competent means that it meets the quality, risk and latency requirements of that decision. There are four kinds of decider: a rule, a model (a predictive model, a decision model that picks one answer from a fixed set, or an optimization solver), an agent built on a large language model (LLM), and a person.

Psychology distinguishes fast, automatic thinking, known as System 1, from slow, deliberate reasoning, known as System 2, and the analogy is useful for routing: rules, models and solvers correspond to System 1, and LLM agents and people to System 2. The distinction is between automatic processing, which follows a fixed procedure, and flexible reasoning and planning, and a solver belongs to the first kind even when it takes minutes to run. It is an analogy and not a taxonomy: the mechanisms are not equivalent to human cognition, and the properties of each decider are tested rather than inferred from the label.

Decisions also move down the tiers over time. Harness research is starting to do this on its own: HarnessMM stores a decision an agent has already made, together with the conditions under which it still holds, and reuses it without calling the model while those conditions hold, cutting tokens by roughly 30 to 88% on coding benchmarks.[51] In a business process those conditions must include that the facts are still current and the policy version has not changed. Each reuse is recorded as a reuse, pointing at the original decision and the conditions it passed, so nobody later mistakes it for fresh reasoning.

Model vendors have begun to use the same two terms for models. A System 1 model, also called a decision model, returns a choice, a score or a probability from a set of answers defined in advance, in one pass, and generates no text. A System 2 model reasons step by step and generates text. In this series the terms describe the tiers of a process, where a tier is one class of decider, and the two kinds of model fall into different tiers.

A decision model stays in the model tier: it is fast, takes no action on its own, returns a prediction with a probability and, when tested with fixed settings, gives the same answer for the same input. A reasoning model only graduates to the agent tier when you give it a role, tools and delegated authority to pursue a goal; reasoning on its own does not make it one. A decision model stays in the model tier even when an agent calls it as a tool. Model size doesn’t change the tier either. A small language model fine-tuned to classify messages or fill in a tool call is a model; give the same small model a role, tools and delegated authority, and it becomes an agent. Small models matter for cost and speed. Much of an agent’s work is narrow, such as parsing a request or producing the structured input a tool expects, and NVIDIA estimates a small model can do it 10 to 30 times more cheaply than a large one.[24] A small model is also cheap and fast enough to run right beside the system of record, inside a tight latency budget. The catch is that each fine-tuned model is one more version to govern, so it is named in every decision record like any other model. In the storm, decision models classify passenger messages, triage expense claims and choose which agent a case goes to, and reasoning models run the itinerary, flight recovery and liaison agents.

A decision model gives a score or a choice, and a score is not a business justification for the action that follows, so two explanations are kept apart. The rule that applies policy to the model's output explains why the decision was made, which is the explanation the trust properties in post 7 require before an action. How a model reached its prediction is explained separately, through its documentation, its calibration and the evaluation of its outcomes, which the sixth trust property covers, and, where a single prediction must be explained, through interpretability methods applied to the model. The hold decision later in this post shows the pattern.

Routing happens through topology, not a central bottleneck. A decision registry maps each decision type to a Kafka topic, and the right decider simply subscribes to it. No central orchestrator sits in the hot path. The message key, which Kafka uses to choose a partition within the topic, keeps the requests for one case in order. The decision record written afterwards names the decider that made the decision and the result. Routing is how the point from posts 1 and 2, that most decisions do not need an agent, is put into practice: in the airline example, most of the 200,000 decision evaluations never reach one.

The agent tier accounts for only 4.5% of the evaluations, but it represents a large workload. Those 9,000 are the evaluations that reach an agent, and the cases they belong to also contain evaluations by rules and models. They belong to the flights, itineraries, bags and claims that remain unresolved for an hour or more, and they are the reason that about 400 cases are open at the peak and that 420 of the 470 agents, those working inside the airline's own operation, are running.

The tiers also look different when they are measured by consequence. The table estimates each tier's share of the money at stake: the financial consequences of such decisions, such as a canceled flight, a block of hotel rooms or a compensation payment. Rules take most of the evaluations, and agents and people take the ones that carry most of the cost.

DeciderShare of evaluationsShare of the money at stake
Rules80%10%
Models and solvers15%25%
LLM agents4.5%40%
People0.5%25%

These shares of money at stake represent exposure, not realized loss, and each decision's exposure is counted once, against whichever tier finally settles it. If a solver proposes a flight swap and an agent resolves the exception, that flight's exposure lands in the agent column. The numbers are illustrative, built to show where risk concentrates.

What this requires
  • Each decision is published as an event that records the context it used, the predictions it relied on, the versions of the model and policy involved and the alternatives it rejected.
  • Routing is based on risk, with explicit rules for escalation to the next tier.
  • A new version of a decision can be tested by replaying history through it before it goes live.
  • Outcomes are joined back to decisions, so that the quality of decisions is measured.
What runs it
  • A business rules engine for the rules tier
  • Apache Flink on Confluent for models that run on streaming features
  • Confluent Streaming Agents,[14] or any enterprise agent platform, for the reasoning tier
  • A design tool in which business owners model, version and simulate processes and the decisions within them

The record below comes from a routine decision in the storm. Flight XA418 is due to depart while 23 of its passengers are still on a delayed inbound flight. A predictive model estimates that the last of the group will reach the gate about six minutes after the door would normally close, and that all 23 can be boarded within eight minutes of the scheduled departure. The rules allow a hold of up to 10 minutes, so a decision service, the software that applies the rules, holds the departure for eight minutes. No agent is involved in this decision, and a record written by an agent has the same form.

JSONA decision record published to the topic flights.decisions.v1. Illustrative. 
{
  "decision_id":    "dec-7f3a91c2",
  "decision_type":  "departure.hold_for_connections",
  "decision_definition": "connection-hold@4.2.0",
  "subject":        { "flight_id": "XA418", "date": "2026-07-14" },
  "decider": {
    "tier":         "rules",
    "decider_id":   "spiffe://airline.example/deciders/connection-hold",
    "on_behalf_of": "role:operations-control"
  },
  "predictions": [
    { "model":  "missed-connection-gbm@2026-06-30",
      "output": { "passengers_at_risk": 23, "shortfall_minutes": 6,
                  "probability_group_misses_connection": 0.93 } }
  ],
  "context": [
    { "topic": "flights.context.v1", "partition": 11, "offset": 88213904 },
    { "topic": "hub.findings.v1",    "partition": 3,  "offset": 5120877 }
  ],
  "context_as_of":  "2026-07-14T19:42:07.311Z",
  "policy_bundle":  "operations-authority@2026.07.1",
  "outcome":        "hold",
  "hold_minutes":   8,
  "alternatives":   [ "no_hold", "escalate" ],
  "authority":      { "limit_minutes": 10 },
  "valid_until":    "2026-07-14T19:47:07Z",
  "causation":      { "caused_by": "evt-5c1e88", "hop": 3 }
}

Four fields deserve explanation. The decider_id identifies whichever rule service, model, agent or person made the decision. Here it uses SPIFFE, an open standard for giving software a verifiable identity, although any verifiable identity scheme would serve. The context field lists the exact positions in the log of the events the decider read, each given as a topic, a partition and an offset. The causation field records which event triggered the decision and how many steps it lies from the original signal, which is the basis for the loop control described in post 2. The predictions field is kept apart from the outcome. A model estimates that 23 passengers are at risk, and that the group has a probability of 0.93 of missing the connection if the flight leaves on time. The probability is meaningful only if the model has been calibrated, which means that its stated probabilities match how often the predicted events occur. The decision service then applies policy and operating limits to choose an action.

The record states what was decided. It does not state that the action was carried out, because that happens later and may fail. Execution is recorded in separate events that are linked to the decision by its identifier, as the action moves through its states: proposed, authorized, requested, accepted, committed, confirmed, failed or compensated. This sequence of linked records is the evidence, and the initial decision is never treated as proof of what followed.

A head start: industry decision packs

The slowest part of a first project is rarely writing the code. Most of the time goes to weeks of meetings sorting out what the decisions are, who owns them and where the data lives. An industry decision pack provides a starting point for one business process. It contains the decisions of that process as models, together with the events and schemas they depend on and the rule sets and model templates that implement them. It also lists the catalog of actions, with their limits and reversibility class, and includes recorded scenarios for testing and the business measures, with a template for the baseline.

A pack is a starting point and is expected to be changed. The client's own policies, limits and systems replace the defaults, and every change is versioned.

What this post established. Every decider reads the same facts as of a stated time, and every decision is an explicit, versioned object routed to the least expensive decider that is competent to make it. Most of the 200,000 evaluations in the storm never reach an agent, and the few that do carry most of the money at stake. Deciding is only half of the problem, though, because nothing changes in the business until a decision becomes an action.

Next in the series

The next post covers the third capability, controlled actions: the action gateway that checks identity, authority, limits and current conditions before anything changes in a system of record, and what it can and cannot guarantee.

Decision engineering · Post 6 of 9

Controlling actions: how the action gateway checks every action before it lands

A decision changes nothing until it becomes an action. This post describes the third capability: how every action is checked for identity, authority, limits and current conditions before it commits, how it is made safe to repeat and the risks specific to agents built on language models.

07Actions

Actions

Definition. An action is a change to a system of record, requested by an identified and authorized decider or execution service. It is performed within a stated limit, in a way that is safe to repeat and, where the nature of the action allows, possible to undo or compensate. The gateway is the sole permitted path for the autonomous actions in scope; people and existing applications may still write to the same systems through their own controls. It can make an action safe to repeat only where the system of record or its adapter supports that, and compensation offsets an action without undoing every consequence that followed it.

What this requires
  • Access to tools follows the principle of least privilege: it is granted to a role and tied to the identity of the agent.
  • Every action carries an idempotency key, which is a unique identifier that allows a repeated request to return the original result without performing the action a second time.
  • Every type of action is classified as reversible, compensable or irreversible. A refund compensates for a payment but does not erase it, and some actions cannot be undone at all. Irreversible actions require stronger authorization before they are executed.
  • Commitments of scarce resources, such as seats, rooms, aircraft and crews, are conditional updates against the system of record, which succeed only if the resource is still in the state the agent last saw, so two agents cannot commit the same resource.
  • Limits on authority and requirements for approval are enforced before the action is executed.
  • Limits on causal chains, budgets and a means of promptly stopping any agent from taking new actions and reconciling the actions it has in flight are in place.
  • The state of long-running work is stored durably, so that it survives a restart.
What runs it
  • An enterprise agent platform that provides the runtime and the catalog of tools
  • An integration and API management layer that supplies the gateway's policy and adapters. A client's existing API or AI gateway is the starting point. The design adds what such gateways usually lack: agent identity with delegated authority, an idempotency ledger (the gateway's record of every action key and its state) with conditional commit, and a decision record for every call. Where the latency or availability of a system of record requires it, the checks run as enforcement points beside that system, following the service mesh pattern: a small enforcement component sits beside each service, rather than one proxy that every call passes through.
  • Confluent as the asynchronous channel that carries requested actions to the gateway and outcomes back to the agents
PseudocodeIllustrative admission logic, not a complete authorization and transaction protocol. Event writing and error handling are omitted, and the policy check, the ledger transitions and the commit are not one atomic transaction. 
def admit(action, credential, registry, policy, ledger, system_of_record):
    identity = verify(credential)                               # proven by the credential,
    agent = registry.lookup(identity)                           # never read from the request

    if agent.revoked or action.hop > agent.max_hops:
        return reject("agent revoked, or causal chain too long")

    if not agent.has_authority_for(action.case_id, action.resource):
        return reject("no delegated authority for this case")

    if action.amount > agent.limit_for(action.tool):
        return escalate("amount exceeds authority")             # route to the next tier

    if not ledger.reserve_budget(agent, action.case_id, action.amount):
        return escalate("cumulative limit reached")              # agent, case and operation totals

    if agent.needs_plan_review(action.tool) and not \
            ledger.approval_valid(digest(action.plan), agent, action.case_id, action.scope):
        return hold("awaiting plan review")

    # Claim the idempotency key in one atomic step (insert if absent).
    # A second request with the same key receives the first result.
    claim = ledger.claim(action.idempotency_key)
    if not claim.is_new:
        if claim.action_digest != digest(action):
            return reject("key reused for a different action")
        if claim.state in ("claimed", "requested", "unknown"):   # an earlier attempt did not finish
            return reconcile(claim, system_of_record)
        if claim.state != "held":
            return claim.result                 # completed earlier: same result again
        # held: the checks above have run again, and the policy checks
        # below run again, under the same key. Only one retry may resume.
        if not ledger.resume(claim):                    # atomic held -> requested
            return reconcile(claim, system_of_record)
    else:
        ledger.mark(action, "requested")                      # durable state before the call

    # Authority and the policy version are checked again here, against
    # the version in force at this moment, before the commit is attempted.
    # policy.current() is the local copy, kept current from the governance
    # log; it is not a call to a policy service on every action. The copy
    # carries its version and the time it was acknowledged.
    pol = policy.current()
    if action.risk in ("irreversible", "high_value"):
        # A recent copy is not enough here (see the policy note below).
        if not (pol.valid_lease_for(action) or
                policy.authoritatively_confirms(action)):
            ledger.mark(action, "held")
            return hold("authorization cannot be confirmed")
    if not pol.permits(agent, action):
        ledger.mark(action, "rejected")            # close the claim, never leave it open
        return reject("authority withdrawn before commit")

    # The system of record applies the change only if the resource
    # is unchanged since the agent read it (compare and swap).
    result = system_of_record.commit_if_version(action, action.seen_version)

    ledger.mark(action, result.status)                        # committed, refused or unknown
    return result

The identity of the requester is established from its credential and is never taken from the request itself. The gateway also confirms that this instance holds delegated authority for the specific case and resource, because an agent can be authenticated and within its limits and still be acting on a booking that is not its own. Because a policy can change while an action is pending, authority is checked again at the moment the action is committed. Safety-critical operational constraints, such as a crew's legality, an aircraft's maintenance status or an airport restriction, are likewise revalidated against their authoritative systems immediately before commitment, because a plan that was valid when approved can be invalid 20 minutes later. Limits are also cumulative. Each action is reserved against running totals for its agent, its case and the whole operation, in the same atomic step as its claim on the ledger, so 30 agents each issuing an allowed voucher cannot together exceed the budget before anyone notices. Guardians spot unusual patterns afterwards; they are not what stops the overspend.

Three further points matter in practice. First, the check and the claim on the idempotency key must be one atomic operation, one that cannot be interrupted halfway; otherwise two workers that each check first and write afterwards can both proceed. The claim is recorded in a ledger, the gateway’s durable record of every key and the state its action has reached. Second, the conditional update is enforced by the system of record itself, since that is the only place where a conflict can be refused with certainty. Third, Kafka's exactly-once guarantees hold right up until you leave Kafka. The moment you call an external reservation or ERP system, networks drop and responses get lost. Beyond the log, you rely on idempotency keys, safe retries and reconciliation against the system of record. In production, every branch of the gateway, including rejected and held actions, writes an event to the log, and any claim left hanging by a crash is reconciled on restart. Logging an unauthorized action doesn't stop it; the gateway has to block it before it takes effect. (I've left the logging, the transaction boundaries and the full authorization protocol out of the code so the order of the checks is easy to follow.) An approval is never accepted from the agent’s own request. The gateway checks it against an independently recorded approval that names the approver and their authority, the plan or action approved as a digest, the scope and the expiry. If the action changes materially after approval, it is approved again.

The policy check deserves its own note. The principle is simple: for a low-risk action, a recent local copy of the policy is enough; for a high-value or irreversible action, the gateway must confirm that permission has not been withdrawn before it proceeds. In detail, the gateway reads policy from a local copy that is synchronized from the governance log, which post 7 describes. A local copy of the policy cannot prove that a revocation approved a moment ago has reached it. A copy is therefore sufficient only when its freshness and revocation guarantees match the risk of the action. The gateway matches the policy check to the risk:

  • Reversible actions rely on a local policy copy synchronized within a few seconds. If a permission was revoked a moment ago, a compensating action offsets it, though it may not undo every consequence that followed.
  • High-value or irreversible actions require a short lease from the policy service: a time-limited confirmation that expires unless it is renewed. The policy service makes a revocation take effect only after outstanding leases expire or are explicitly canceled. Without a valid lease, the gateway checks the governance log directly, and if it can't, it fails closed and holds the action.

A rejected action closes its claim in the ledger, so that no claim is left in an unfinished state. A held action keeps its claim in the held state, and when the hold is lifted, the workflow that owns the case resubmits it with the same idempotency key, so the resumed action cannot commit twice.

Conditional commits require the system of record to support optimistic locking (refusing an update if the record changed since you read it). Plenty of legacy systems don't. When a legacy mainframe simply overwrites whatever update it receives, you have to put a reservation adapter in front of it. Without it, the gateway alone cannot promise that two agents will never commit the same resource.

Card networks have already shipped this for one domain. Mastercard’s Agent Pay issues tokens with transaction-level limits and validity windows and keeps an audit trail for disputes;[28] Google’s AP2 uses signed mandates for intent, cart and payment;[29] Stripe’s shared payment tokens are scoped to one seller, one amount and an expiry measured in minutes.[30] That is a policy lease, a budget reservation and an approval record in one artifact. The gateway generalizes it to every system of record.

These are not hypothetical. In July 2025 a coding agent deleted a production database despite a written instruction to stop,[31] and in April 2026 another used a root-scoped token it found in an unrelated file to delete a production volume and its backups.[32] Neither system had a conditional commit or a scoped, expiring authority between the agent and the store.

Coding tools are moving the same way. Anthropic's auto mode for Claude Code replaces most approval prompts with a separate classifier, partly because people approved 93% of them anyway. The classifier never sees what the agent read, so text injected into a file or web page cannot argue its way past it. Anthropic also publishes the miss rate: the check still let through 17% of the real overeager actions it was tested on, and the company says it is not a replacement for careful review on high-stakes systems.[48] That is the case for hard limits and conditional commits. A model checking another model reduces the risk; it does not bound it.

Risks specific to language-model agents

The controls above address operational risks such as excess authority, duplicate actions and failed recovery. Agents based on language models add risks of their own, and four rules follow from them.

  • Everything an agent reads is treated as untrusted, because documents, messages and the responses of tools can contain instructions that were planted to redirect the agent. Such content is handled as data and never as a command.
  • Permissions do not depend on the prompt. What an agent may do is decided by its registration and enforced at the gateway, and no instruction to the agent, from any source, can widen it.
  • Consequential decisions are validated independently, because an agent may reason incorrectly or pass wrong arguments to a tool. Rules check its proposals, and a second decider reviews those with large consequences.
  • Agents are tested against misuse as well as error. Evaluation covers accidental failure, deliberate manipulation by outside parties or other agents, and the leakage of sensitive information.

A credential broker protects the key, not the call. Christian Posta’s series on credential injection for agents makes the case that an agent should never hold a credential, and that the gateway should inject a short-lived one just in time.[46] That is right, and it is not enough: as Shan Huang put it in the discussion of that series, a prompt-injected agent never has to steal a credential; it just phrases the request politely. That is why the gateway checks the action, for this case, within these limits, against the live state, and not only the caller.

Google's Agent Compute Engine, announced in October 2026, takes the same line at cloud scale: no secrets inside the agent's sandbox, a token swapped in at the gateway, and a check of the user's delegation, the agent's identity and the machine's on every outbound call.[50] That protects the key and the connection. Whether this booking belongs to this case and fits this agent's limit is still the action gateway's job.

What this post established. The shared log, the explicit decision and the gateway each do one job, and none of them does the others’. The log gives every decider the same facts as of a stated time, but it does not stop two agents committing the same seat; only a conditional update at the system of record does that. The gateway proves identity and checks authority at the moment of commit, but it cannot make a legacy system transactional, and a policy copy is only as current as its acknowledged version. What the series guarantees is bounded by those mechanisms.

Next in the series

The next post covers the fourth capability, trust. It defines a trusted decision by six properties and describes how agents are managed, how governance is published as a stream, how decisions are replayed and how trust extends to other organizations' agents.

Decision engineering · Post 7 of 9

Proving trust: how to show that each decision can be trusted

This post defines a trusted decision by six properties. It then describes how agents are registered and managed, how governance is published as a stream, how decisions are replayed and audited and how trust extends to agents that other organizations run.

08Trust

Trust

Definition. People trust one another on the basis of identity, credentials issued by a recognized authority, reputation and a record of past behavior. Trust in agents is built by analogy to those foundations, with the difference that each has to be an enforced mechanism rather than a judgment. Decision engineering turns the parts of that which can be engineered into measurable mechanisms. Five of the six properties below concern control and accountability, and the sixth concerns whether the decision was a good one, because a decision can be fully controlled and still be wrong:

PropertyMechanismMeasure
AttributableEvery event carries the verifiable identity of the decider or service that produced it, and the chain of delegation that leads back to an accountable person.The share of actions that have a verified identity and a named owner. The target is 100%.
Explainable before the actionThe agent publishes a plan, and the plan is reviewed in proportion to the risk: automatically against policy for routine actions, and by a second agent or a person for actions that are irreversible or have large consequences. A plan states what the agent intends to do. It is not proof that the reasoning behind it is correct, so it is checked against policy and supporting evidence. The form varies by decider: a rule has readable conditions and a policy justification, a model has a validated output and the rule applied to it, an agent has a reviewable plan, and a person has a recorded approval and rationale.The share of consequential decisions with a recorded justification and the review or approval that their risk level requires, and the rate at which executed actions differ from what was authorized.
Reconstructable after the action, and reproducible where the decider allowsThe decision record identifies the exact context and versions that were used, and that evidence is preserved.For rules, models and solvers run with fixed random seeds and deterministic settings, so that the same run gives the same result, the share of decisions that re-execute to the same outcome, which should approach 100%. For LLM agents, the share of decisions whose evidence can be fully reconstructed; a fresh run is not expected to match, and its agreement rate is reported as a test result rather than a requirement.
BoundedLimits on authority, spending, rate and the length of causal chains are enforced before execution.The number of breaches blocked before execution compared with the number discovered afterwards.
Reversible where possibleEvery type of action is classified as reversible, compensable or irreversible. Compensating actions are tested, irreversible actions require stronger authorization, and every agent can be stopped. Stopping an agent prevents further actions; its actions in flight are checked and reconciled, and its committed actions are compensated where that is possible.The share of action types that are classified and, where compensation exists, tested, and the time needed to revoke an agent.
EvaluatedInputs are validated, outcomes are joined to decisions, and each type of decision is evaluated continuously against its business objective and its policy.The share of decisions later overridden or reversed, the outcomes achieved against the objective, and how well stated confidence matches actual results.

The sixth property deserves emphasis. A decision can comply with its policy, execute without error and be fully auditable, and still be unfair or commercially poor. Evaluation therefore covers four things: the errors of the predictions; drift in the models; differences in outcomes between groups of people affected; and overrides and appeals, with how they were resolved. It also covers human review wherever law or policy requires it.

Take the eight-minute hold of flight XA418 from post 5. It passes the first five properties. Whether it was a good decision needs three more facts: 21 of the 23 passengers made it; the aircraft missed its slot and left 19 minutes late, which cost more than the hotel rooms the hold avoided; and groups the model scored at 0.93 missed their connection 90% of the time, so the model was well calibrated and the policy is what needs review. None of that is in the decision record alone. It comes from joining the record to what happened next. (Illustrative figures.)

Some outcomes can be counted, like those 21 passengers. Many can only be judged: did the agent stay inside its authority, did it treat the partner's message as data, was the plan sensible? More and more of that judging is done by models grading other models against a written rubric. That works under four conditions. First, a failed critical rubric, such as a commitment above the agent's limit, fails the whole case; nine good scores never average it away. Second, the rubric set, the judge model and its prompt are versioned and recorded, so the same verdict can be reproduced later. Third, a case goes to a person when the judges disagree, not when a judge says it is unsure, because model judges are often confidently wrong. Fourth, a person also reviews a random sample of the confident verdicts, which is the only way to measure how often the judges themselves miss. The open decision record in post 8 carries all of this in its evaluation record, next to the outcome.

Agents need lifecycle management

A fleet of agents needs the same lifecycle discipline as a workforce: onboarding, a defined role, an accountable human owner, periodic reviews and a clean way to revoke access when an agent misbehaves. Every agent definition is registered before any instance of it is allowed to connect, and four levels are kept distinct: the definition sets what a kind of agent may do, the running instance has its own authenticated identity, the delegated authority covers one business case and the individual action is taken under that authority. The registration is itself published as an event, so the history of which agents were permitted to do what can be replayed like everything else.

YAMLAn agent registration. Illustrative. 
kind: AgentRegistration
metadata:
  name: itinerary-agent
  owner: customer-recovery@airline.example     # the accountable team
  certified_by: operations-risk                # the authority that approved it
  expires: 2027-01-31                          # recertify or retire by this date
identity:
  spiffe_id: spiffe://airline.example/agents/itinerary-agent   # the definition
  instance_identity: issued_at_start           # one per running instance
  case_authority: delegated_per_case           # expires when the case closes
  acts_on_behalf_of: role:customer-recovery
role:
  consumes: [hub.findings.v1, flights.decisions.v1]
  produces: [itineraries.decisions.v1]
  tools:
    - name: reservations.read
    - name: reservations.rebook                # own flights only
    - name: vouchers.issue
      limit: { amount: 300, currency: USD, per: passenger }
      requires: plan_review
limits:
  max_hops: 6
  token_budget_per_task: 200000
  rate: 30 actions/minute
oversight:
  # levels: 0 manual | 1 assisted | 2 recommend | 3 supervised | 4 bounded | 5 full
  autonomy: 4                                  # the highest level this agent may act at
  review_sample: 0.05
  control_topic: agents.control.v1             # used to stop the agent

The autonomy field in the registration puts the principle of earned trust into practice. It uses the six levels of autonomy set out in the brief, from 0 (manual) to 5 (full), and records the highest level at which this agent may act; each decision type also has its own ceiling, and the lower of the two applies. Before an agent is first given authority, and again before each promotion, it runs in parallel: it decides beside the existing process on live volume, and its decisions are logged and compared but not acted on. It moves up a level only on evidence: complete decision records, agreement with actual outcomes, no unauthorized action committed and every blocked attempt investigated and resolved. A rule or a model must also pass its reproducibility tests. For an agent, the replay agreement rate is reported as diagnostic evidence, and promotion rests on approved scenarios, decision quality and policy compliance. Promotion also needs an accountable approval under the enterprise's risk policy, because an agent can perform well and still carry an unresolved security, legal or fairness risk. Demotion, by contrast, can follow from evidence alone. Certification of the definition and the short-lived authority delegated to each instance are kept distinct. A change to an agent's harness, like a change to its model, creates a new version of the definition, which runs in parallel again before it acts.[18]

Autonomy ladders are now common. Gartner’s four levels (May 2026) are assigned at design time;[33] AWS’s graduated autonomy (August 2026) is earned: every agent starts in probation, scores over a rolling 50-action window, and a high operator rejection rate caps its safety score.[34] What this series adds is what the evidence should be: outcomes from replay and the chaos tests, not an accuracy composite, and a ceiling set by how reversible the action is.

Governance as a stream

The decision record shows what was decided, but a regulator will also ask what the rules were at that moment. An auditor may ask, for example, who was able to see the customer data that trained a pricing model at noon on June 24, and who actually did. Those are two questions: the first is answered from the history of access policy, and the second needs independently verified access logs. Many enterprises hold the history in several governance systems, and the gap is rebuilding one consistent, verifiable view of the state on an earlier date.

The remedy is to treat changes in governance as events. When a policy is edited, a field is reclassified, access is granted, a model is promoted, consent is withdrawn, a schema changes or an agent is registered, that change is published to a governance log: a dedicated topic on the same event backbone, the shared streaming infrastructure that carries the business data. Two benefits follow. First, the decision loop, the fast path that makes decisions in the moment, reads the policy version in force directly from this log, so an approved change can take effect without a software release; propagation within seconds is a design target. Each decision service acknowledges the version it has loaded, and a service that cannot confirm that it holds the current version holds or escalates its decisions until it can.

Second, the state of governance on any past date within the retained history can be reconstructed by reading the log up to that date, provided each change carries its effective time and the history is complete.

Knowing that an agent's limit rose from $200 to $500 does not tell you whether it later spent $600. Governance therefore takes three parts, and governance latency drops only when all three work together:

  • History establishes which policies and permissions applied, and when. The governance log provides it.
  • Enforcement checks each action against those controls before it is executed. The action gateway provides it.
  • Monitoring compares the actions that were actually taken with the policy in force at the time, continuously, and raises an exception when they disagree or when evidence is missing. A stream processing job that joins the action records to the governance log provides it.

A change to a policy passes through five steps.

  1. DefineThe policy is written as code, kept under version control and reviewed in the same way as software.
  2. ValidateAutomated checks test the policy, including a simulation against recent decisions.
  3. ApproveA named approver signs off, and, as one illustrative control, a change to a threshold requires two people.
  4. PublishThe new version is written to the governance log with its version number, its approvers and the time.
  5. ApplyThe decision loop picks up the new version from the log, and every later decision record names it.

The first three steps run in the learning loop, the slower cycle in the lakehouse that reviews outcomes, the fourth is the governance log and the fifth is the decision loop.

The governance log is kept in three layers. The live topic on Confluent serves the decision loop and holds recent history. The same stream is written to the lakehouse as an append-only table, and that table serves as the long-term governance log. A question about a past decision is then answered by joining its decision record to the governance log as of the time of the decision. The third layer is the audit controls described in post 8, because writing a stream to a table does not by itself create a compliant archive. Two details need care. The long-term log must be an append-only table of events, since the version history that lakehouse tables keep automatically is usually pruned after a limited period. The evidence must also have access controls that are separate from those of the learning data, so that the people who retrain models cannot alter the audit record.

Lakehouse pipelines can now be rewound. Databricks Lakeflow restores a pipeline’s table versions, stream offsets and operator state to a point in the last seven days, and the next run reprocesses from there.[45] That is the right tool for the long-term copies: if the job that joins decision records to policy versions is wrong, rewind it and run it again. It is the wrong tool for the governance log itself, which is never rewound; a policy rollback is a new event that points at an old version. And because rewind does not undo anything outside the pipeline, replaying the decision loop still goes through the simulated gateway.

Guardians watch the decision stream

A guardian is a verifier that watches a stream of decisions and acts when something is at risk. It does not make the business decisions itself, although each intervention it makes is recorded as a decision. A guardian template is a ready-made guardian for one kind of risk, which a project configures with its own limits and policies. Most guardians are rules or small models, because the things they watch are structured, such as spending totals, decision counts and policy versions. A guardian needs a language model only to review free text or a consequential plan, and at that point it is one of the agents described in post 5. Gartner calls these guardian agents and expects them to be 10 to 15% of the agentic market by 2030;[42] OWASP’s agent control standard places them around every agent. The six templates below are a decomposition of that idea.

While the action gateway checks each action individually before it executes, guardians are the continuous monitoring layer of governance described above, watching the stream for patterns that no single check can see, such as an agent repeating an action, a model drifting or a record that is missing. They act through two channels: the control topic, where an agent receives the instruction to stop, and the gateway, which can stop an agent, lower its autonomy or raise an exception for its owner. Like observers, guardians are not counted among the 470 agents in the storm. Nor does the roster have a separate reviewing agent. In the storm, the checks come from rules, from maintenance agents that can refuse an aircraft swap, from recovery coordination agents that find conflicts between proposals, and from the duty manager who approves the plan.

Guardian templateWhat it watchesWhat it doesDecider type
Limit guardianSpending, rates and repeated actions by each agent, across many actionsStops the agent through the control topic when a limit is breached, and reconciles its unfinished claimsRule
Policy guardianActions that were taken, compared with the policy version in force at the timeRaises an exception for the owner and, if the pattern recurs, stops the agentRule
Loop guardianChains of events that feed themselves across several agentsStops the agents in the chain and lowers their autonomy until the cause is foundRule
Evidence guardianActions in systems of record that have no matching decision record, found by reconciliation, and records that are incompleteRaises an exception for the ownerRule
Drift guardianPrediction error, calibration and the rate of overrides and reversals for each type of decisionSuspends the model or reroutes the decision to an approved fallback until the model is reviewed, and triggers a replay test of the decisionModel
Plan guardianConsequential plans that exceed an agent's authoritySends the plan to a second agent or a person for reviewAgent, or person

Each intervention is itself a decision, recorded in the same way as any other, and each guardian is registered with an owner and an expiry date, like the agents it watches. Its thresholds are versioned and approved through the policy lifecycle described above.

Replay supports audit and decision assurance

Suppose that three months after the disruption a regulator asks why flight XA418 was held for eight minutes, and whether the decision followed the rules in force at the time. The decision record identifies the positions in the log that the decider read, and those events have been preserved, together with the versions of the rules and models that were applied. The preserved evidence allows the decision to be reconstructed and, where the decider is deterministic, its logic to be run again.

PythonReproducing a decision from its record. Illustrative. 
from confluent_kafka import Consumer, TopicPartition

def replay(decision, load_decider):
    c = Consumer({"bootstrap.servers": BROKERS, "group.id": "audit-replay",
                  "enable.auto.commit": False})
    context = []
    for ref in decision["context"]:
        c.assign([TopicPartition(ref["topic"], ref["partition"], ref["offset"])])
        msg = c.poll(10.0)
        if msg is not None and not msg.error() and msg.offset() == ref["offset"]:
            event = msg.value()                       # still within the log's retention
        else:
            event = archive.read(ref)                 # past retention: the preserved copy,
                                                      # verified against its recorded digest
        if event is None:
            raise EvidenceMissing(ref)                # report the gap, never substitute
        context.append(event)                         # the exact event the decider read
    # Features, prompts and tool responses are loaded from the evidence
    # store in the same way, and each is checked against its recorded digest.

    decider = load_decider(decision["decision_definition"], decision["policy_bundle"])
    again = decider.decide(context)
    return again.outcome == decision["outcome"], again

Replay is not a new idea. OWASP’s agentic top ten already recommends re-running the last week’s recorded actions in a production clone before a policy change,[43] and reconstruction and re-execution exist in products. What-if replay of past decisions against a new policy does not, and that is the one this section builds toward. Three operations are often confused under the name of replay. Reconstruction establishes which information, policies and models were used. Re-execution runs the same decision logic again on the preserved inputs, where that is feasible. Simulation estimates what would have happened under a different decision, and it depends on assumptions that must be validated separately. Positions in the event log are not the whole context of a decision: reconstruction may also need the versions of derived features, the prompts, the responses of tools, the model settings, the version of the agent's harness and any external data used, so these are preserved as part of the evidence. None of the three operations shows that a decision was right, because an incorrect decision can be re-executed perfectly. That judgment comes from the evaluation of outcomes described in the table above.

The limits of replay. Rules reproduce their results exactly, and models and solvers do so when they are run with fixed seeds and deterministic settings, since a solver with a time limit or a parallel search can return a different plan on each run. An LLM agent may not produce the same text twice, even when it is given the same inputs. For the agent tier, replay establishes three things: that the inputs were those stated in the record, that the policy checks pass again, and that a fresh run reaches the same outcome at a measured rate. The plan and the output of the agent are stored as events for the same reason. A low replay agreement rate for a type of decision is a reason to move that decision to a lower, more deterministic tier.

From audit to design: what-if

Replay is not only a tool for audit; the same capability also serves design. A business owner selects a recorded period, changes one element of a decision, such as a limit, a rule or a model version, and runs the recorded events through the changed decision. Actions are sent to a simulated gateway, so nothing in the live operation is affected. A changed decision also changes what happens next: a longer hold affects gates, crews, later flights and the choices of passengers. Recorded events cannot show those effects, so they are estimated with a simulation model of the operation, which in the airline example is the digital twin, and the assumptions of that model must be validated separately. The results are then compared with what was recorded.

The comparison makes the trade-off visible before any change is released: fewer missed connections and hotel nights, at the price of longer delays that spread to later flights. The same capability has three uses: it tests a change before release, it supports the investigation of a past decision, and it provides a safe environment in which to evaluate an agent before it is given authority. In the airline example it is also how the digital twin moves from simulation to decision, because the twin and the live operation share the same operational data.

Trust must be federated

Authentication proves who the partner's agent is, not that its airline will honor the discount it offers. Trust the identity, verify the offer. At this scale no person can vouch for each agent individually, and many of the agents involved belong to other organizations. The certification of agents across organizations is still an emerging area, and this part of the framework is a proposal. I expect trust to be delegated to authorities that certify agents against a standard, much as the UL and CSA marks do for physical products. Inside the enterprise, that authority is typically the risk or security function. Between enterprises, it is likely to be an independent third party. Before the airline relies on any external offer, it confirms the terms directly against the partner's systems. The log does not replace these authorities; it provides what they need in order to certify: events tied to identities, a durable record of plans and actions, and enforced schemas and access controls.

What this post established. A trusted decision is one whose evidence passes six tests, and the sixth, whether the decision was a good one, is the one most often forgotten. Agents earn autonomy level by level on evidence, governance changes are published as events so that the rules in force on any date can be rebuilt, replay comes in three kinds, none of which proves that a decision was right, and trust in other organizations' agents rests on authorities that certify them.
