Decision engineering · Post 8 of 9

Keeping the evidence: how decision records outlast the log and shape the architecture

A trusted decision needs evidence that outlasts the event log. This post covers what the event log can and can't do, where systems of record fit, what regulators expect and the reference architecture that brings the pieces together.

09Evidence

Evidence that outlasts the log

What the log provides, and what it does not

An event log does not make decisions trustworthy on its own, and its guarantees should be stated precisely. Apache Kafka preserves the order of events within a partition, but not across partitions or topics. How long events are kept is a matter of configuration, and a topic can be set to keep only the latest record for each key, which removes earlier versions. The log only proves what was written down, not that the data was true or the action was authorized. That's why I separate three layers:

  • The event backbone moves and processes operational information in real time.
  • The decision evidence consists of the decision records, the references to the context they used, the policies and approvals that applied and the outcomes of the actions.
  • The audit controls preserve that evidence for the required period and allow it to be verified independently. They include retention that matches the audit period, restricted administrative access, a copy of the evidence in a lakehouse in open table formats that any analytics tool can read, and a means of detecting alteration.

The middle layer is the one every platform lacks. Agent platforms now record what the agent did. The decision record is different: it records what was decided, against which inputs, which policy version and which approver. A trace tells you the agent called the booking tool; the record tells you whether it was allowed to.

Systems of record, regulatory evidence and decision lineage

Decision engineering does not replace an enterprise's systems of record or its obligations to keep records. The distinction matters because a decision, its execution and its result are three separate facts. Suppose that an agent decides a passenger is due a $300 hotel voucher. The decision is that the voucher should be issued. The execution is that the voucher service accepted the request. The business state is that the finance system shows the voucher as issued. These facts arise at different moments, and they may not agree. If the voucher service times out, the decision log records only what was intended; the passenger still has no room. That's why the architecture separates four distinct roles:

1 · Systems of recordReservations, departure control, crew, financeRemain authoritative for business transactions and their results.
2 · Event backboneConfluentCarries signals, changes in context, decisions, requested actions and confirmed outcomes in real time.
3 · Decision lineageA searchable repositoryHolds each decision with its source references, model and policy versions, approvals and outcomes.
4 · Evidence archiveRegulated retentionPreserves evidence for the required period with tamper evidence, legal holds and controlled access, and can be verified independently.

The event backbone can retain records for a long time, but it should not be assumed to be the regulated evidence archive, a role that requires its own design and verification. The decision lineage repository and the evidence archive can both be held in a lakehouse, provided that they are separate tables with separate controls.

Reconciliation. Every recorded action is checked against the system of record that carried it out, and the result of that check becomes part of the evidence. A decision whose action cannot be confirmed is raised as an exception.

Decision lineage and data lineage. Data lineage explains where information came from and how it was transformed. Decision lineage explains how that information contributed to a particular decision, which model and policy were applied, and what happened afterwards. A position in the event log shows where an event appeared, not where the information originated or whether it was correct. For a consequential decision, the evidence should answer the questions in the following table.

EvidenceQuestion it must answer
Source provenanceWhere did each input originate, and was that source authoritative?
Data processingWhich transformations, joins and enrichments were applied?
Decision contextWhat information was actually available when the decision was made?
Model and policyWhich exact versions, configurations and rules were applied?
ResponsibilityWhich agent, person or service acted, and under what authority?
ExecutionWas the action requested, accepted, committed, rejected or reversed?
ReconciliationDoes the recorded outcome agree with the system of record?
IntegrityCan the evidence be verified independently as complete and unaltered?

Privacy and retention. Retaining context so that decisions can be reconstructed has a cost, because it can increase the amount of sensitive data held across the enterprise. The principle is to capture enough evidence to establish what happened without keeping a permanent copy of every sensitive input. A decision record can hold a pseudonymous identifier, along with the versions that applied and a protected reference to the underlying data. It can also hold a cryptographic digest of each input, although a predictable input can still be guessed from its digest. The sensitive data itself stays in governed repositories with their own retention and access controls, and retention periods are set according to the purpose of the data. Encrypting each person's data with a separate key that can be deleted is a useful technique for erasure, but not a complete answer, because copies, derived attributes, backups and replicated topics must be addressed as well.

Regulation. Requirements for evidence differ by industry and jurisdiction, and they must be mapped for each deployment. In the European Union, the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) sets principles of purpose limitation, data minimization and storage limitation. It also sets rights concerning erasure and solely automated decisions, and the AI Act sets logging and record-keeping duties for high-risk systems.

Such duties apply to particular uses, and they do not mean that every automated business decision needs the same records or the same retention. For broker-dealers and other entities it covers in the United States, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Rule 17a-4 sets conditions for electronic records that storage in an event log does not meet by itself. Neither the SEC nor FINRA has said whether an agent’s actions are records under it, so treating them as records is prudence rather than settled law. FINRA’s 2026 oversight report already warns that agent action chains “may be difficult to reconstruct, complicating auditability.”[27]

The enforcement is ahead of the mechanism. In August 2026 the Dutch data protection authority fined Uber 824.99 million euros for fully automated driver deactivations with no meaningful human involvement.[35] The evidential questions were whether a person was involved and whether the driver was told, which is exactly what approval and decision records prove. Colorado’s revised AI law and California’s automated decision rules both take effect on January 1, 2027, and both require records showing where automated decisions were used.[36][37]

Rules on data residency and cross-border transfer determine where evidence may be held and who may access it. Legal discovery raises further questions of access, disclosure, legal holds and privileged information. This post does not offer legal advice. The architectural point is that the design keeps operational event processing separate from the long-term preservation of evidence, so that each can meet its own requirements.

RequirementWhat it asks of the evidenceWhere the architecture meets it
GDPR (European Union)Purpose limitation, data minimization and storage limitation, plus rights concerning erasure and solely automated decisionsDecision records hold pseudonymous identifiers, versions and protected references rather than copies of sensitive inputs; the data itself stays in governed repositories with their own retention; human review where law requires it
EU AI ActLogging and human-oversight duties for most high-risk systems, which now apply from December 2, 2027 after the 2026 Digital Omnibus[26]Decision records, the governance log and the evidence archive, retained for the required period
SEC Rule 17a-4 (United States)Conditions for electronic records of broker-dealers and other covered entities, which storage in an event log does not meet by itselfAn evidence archive designed and verified for those conditions, kept separate from operational event processing
Data residency and cross-border transferWhere evidence may be held and who may access itThe location and access controls of the evidence archive, set for each deployment
Legal discoveryAccess, disclosure, legal holds and privileged informationLegal holds and controlled access in the evidence archive

A summary of the obligations named above, mapped to the architecture. Requirements must be mapped for each deployment, and this is not legal advice.

Completeness and correctness. Decision lineage makes the sequence of events open to inspection, but it does not certify that a decision was correct, authorized or based on true information. Evidence must also be complete: the enterprise must be able to show which decisions were made, detect any decision with no record, and verify the integrity of what is preserved. Logging alone does not establish this, and reconciliation with the systems of record is one of the checks that does.

The systems of record remain authoritative for business transactions. The decision record explains what was proposed, why it was permitted, what action was requested and what the systems of record confirmed. The evidence archive preserves what is needed to verify those facts.

This separation allows an enterprise to benefit from real-time autonomous decisions while keeping its established responsibilities for data governance, records management, audit and regulatory compliance. Decision lineage also gives risk, compliance, data and internal audit leaders a reason to support the architecture.

A common format for recording business decisions

A standard for modeling decisions already exists. Decision Model and Notation (DMN), published by the Object Management Group, defines how to draw the structure of a decision and how to express its logic, most often as a decision table. Figure 8.1 shows the decision to hold a departure, which post 5 introduced, in this form.

Any case that no earlier rule covers, including one with missing information, an illegal crew or no available slot, is escalated to a person and is never approved by default. The table decides only whether to hold for connections. Permission to depart remains subject to separate safety, crew, air traffic and operational checks.

DMN defines the structure and logic of a decision and how that logic is evaluated, which is why the table above can be run. What it does not define is the record of each time a decision runs: the context that was read, the authority that applied, the execution and its confirmed outcome. DMN was also published before agents became deciders. (Note the naming collision: in DMN, a “decision model” is the definition of a business decision and its logic, not the System 1 decision model from post 5.) The open decision record, the common format described above, complements DMN by recording what happened each time a decision ran. Each record names the model and version that produced it and adds what DMN does not cover: the context that was read, the identity and authority of the decider, the alternatives rejected and links to the records of the action and its confirmed outcome. The record travels in a standard event envelope, such as CloudEvents, so that it can move across different platforms. A common schema, versioning rules and agreed definitions of the decision and execution states are what allow systems to exchange evidence consistently. DMN and CloudEvents are established standards. The decision record is a proposed vendor-neutral schema that makes run-time evidence interoperable; it is not yet an open standard, and formal standardization would be a separate step.

DMN already definesThe open decision record adds
The structure of a decision: which decisions and inputs it depends onThe exact context that was read, as positions in the event log
The logic of a decision, as decision tables and expressionsWhich kind of decider made it, including a model, an agent or a person, with its identity
Names and versions of decision models, DMN’s term for the definition of a decisionThe authority that applied, the predictions that were relied on and the alternatives that were rejected
A format for exchanging models between toolsLinks to the separate records of the action and its confirmed outcome, so that quality can be measured

The value of a vendor-neutral format, once it is published and adopted, is that records can come from any source. A rules engine, an agent framework, a workflow engine and a person using a screen can all publish the same record, and a single body of evidence results. A client who adopts it is not tied to one vendor's tools, although that benefit depends on the specification being published and taken up beyond the people who wrote it, the separate step noted above.

11The architecture

Reference architecture

Figure 2.4 gave the map; this is the same architecture in full. It is organized in planes, each a group of components with one role, and it places the event log at the center. The planes divide into a control plane and a data path. The trust plane and the governance log are the control plane: they decide what may run where and under what policy, and they publish those decisions to the rest. The event backbone, the deciders, the gateway enforcement points and the systems of record are the data path, which carries each decision and action. The log is the common coordination point; context services, workflow state, gateway enforcement points and the systems of record are shared dependencies of their own, and each needs its own availability design. Source systems publish events to the log. Deciders read context from it and publish decisions to it. The action gateway reads requested actions from it and publishes their outcomes. A trust plane enforces policy on events as they are written and collects evidence from them afterwards, and a learn plane receives all events for history, simulation and improvement. The decision loop runs on the backbone, and the learning loop runs in the learn plane.

PlaneRoleComponents
Event backboneProvides the shared, ordered and retained record, performs stateful processing and serves current context to deciders.Confluent Cloud or Confluent Platform for Apache Kafka, Apache Flink, the schema registry with data contracts and stream lineage. Confluent Cloud additionally provides the managed Real-Time Context Engine and Tableflow; a self-managed deployment needs separately chosen components for those two roles
DecidersMake each decision at the least expensive competent tier and publish a decision record.A business rules engine, models running on Flink or behind a model serving platform, optimization solvers, Confluent Streaming Agents or an enterprise agent platform, and people
Action gatewayServes as the only route into systems of record and enforces identity, limits, conditional commitment of resources, safe repetition and compensation. A durable workflow component beside it owns the state of long-running cases, including retries, timeouts and the running of compensating actions.An integration and API management layer, with a durable workflow engine for process state
Trust planeManages agent identity and secrets, the agent registry and lifecycle, policy and monitoring, and holds the decision lineage repository and the evidence archive.An identity provider, a secrets manager, an agent control plane[3] and an AI governance platform
Learn planeRuns the learning loop. It holds long-term history, including the long-term copy of the governance log, and supports model training, policy review, simulation and analytics, with pipeline rewind and replay for the derived tables.A lakehouse such as Databricks or Snowflake

In the airline example, the digital twin and the live decision systems share the same operational data. Live decisions use the latest validated information, while the twin maintains a model of the operation, with its dependencies and constraints, that supports simulation. Proposed changes can therefore be tested against a common operational history, without assuming that replaying history can predict every consequence.

Placing the log at the center does not make it the authority for everything. Three requirements are met by three different capabilities, and the architecture integrates them without replacing any of them. Nor does every decision need the full architecture. A low-risk decision inside one application can keep its existing controls and publish only its decision records.

RequirementCapability responsible
Share changing information across systemsEvent streaming and integration
Execute business transactions with authoritySystems of record and controlled APIs
Preserve and verify the evidence of decisionsDecision records, reconciliation and governed retention

Four design rules follow from this architecture. First, agents never hold credentials for systems of record, so the gateway is the only component able to change them; knowing the current state of a resource and having the authority to change it are kept separate. The IETF’s Credential Broker for Agents draft (March 2026) makes the same rule the center of its design and adds one worth adopting: the service that decides policy and the service that holds credentials are never the same component.[47] Second, no component is trusted because of where it runs. An event is accepted only from an authenticated and authorized producer that satisfies the required data contract, and the producer's verified identity is recorded with it. Third, synchronous calls, in which the caller waits for the answer, are still permitted where an immediate answer is needed, such as a tool call through the gateway, but every one is recorded on the log as a request and an outcome. Fourth, operational systems remain the systems of record for business transactions, and every outcome recorded on the log is reconciled with them.

The gateway in these rules is a logical enforcement layer, not one application or one network endpoint. It can run as the client's existing API or AI gateway together with instances and adapters close to the systems they protect, all applying the same policy. If a gateway enforcement point is unavailable, the actions it protects cannot proceed. If the central policy service is unavailable, an action proceeds only where its risk policy accepts a valid local copy or an unexpired lease; every other action is held or escalated. For processes that cannot wait, an explicitly authorized manual recovery procedure is part of the design, and its use is recorded like any other action. Two kinds of failure are treated differently. If a model server goes down, a decider can fall back to a cached model or rule, because a slightly stale prediction is a known, logged risk. If the authority in force can't be confirmed, the action stops, because acting on stale authority creates direct regulatory exposure.

This split follows a published case. Netflix removed the central proxy from the request path of its model serving platform, which as of 2025 served hundreds of model types at a million requests a second for more than 30 client services. The proxy had become a shared dependency whose failure degraded many experiences at once, and it added 10 to 20 milliseconds to each request for serializing the payload, more for the slowest requests. Netflix kept the routing rules in a control plane that publishes them to the proxies beside each service, and chose availability over consistency, because a stale routing rule is harmless.[17] The gateway here keeps the same shape but makes the opposite choice on authority, for the reason given above. The Netflix case supports removing an unnecessary proxy from a latency-sensitive path; it does not show that an action gateway can adopt the same trade-offs where consistency of authority matters more than availability.

What this post established. The log is necessary and not sufficient. It orders events within a partition, keeps them for as long as it is configured to, and shows what was recorded, not that the record was true or the action authorized. Therefore, trust rests on evidence outside the log: the decision record joined to the governance log as of the decision time, the confirmation from the system of record, and audit controls that preserve both and can be verified independently. The six properties are tests of that evidence. A decision can pass the first five and still produce a poor outcome, which is why the sixth measures decision quality and business results, not only whether the controls worked.

Decision engineering · Post 9 of 9

Getting started: where this fits and what to do in the first 90 days

This post looks at what the market is building, where today's tools stop and where decision engineering fits. It ends with a 90-day plan, starting from the first decision you pick to focus on.

12The market

What the market is doing

  • Confluent is now part of IBM. IBM completed its acquisition of Confluent on March 17, 2026, and described the combined portfolio as providing trusted communication and data flow for generative and agentic AI.[1]
  • Streaming vendors are extending into context and agents. Confluent's Real-Time Context Engine is generally available and serves current context to agents through MCP.[2] Redpanda’s Agentic Data Plane, which the company positions as a governed access layer that mediates every interaction between agents and data, reached general availability in June 2026.[5]
  • Agent platforms are adding control planes. During 2026, agent platforms introduced central consoles for registering, operating and governing agents, together with runtime monitoring of agent behavior.[3][4] In October 2026, AWS described a layered approach it calls Trust in Depth: policy is enforced on every tool call outside the agent’s own reasoning, and an agent is given more autonomy as evidence builds that its actions can be verified.[19]
  • Cloud providers are building the agent runtime. In October 2026 Google described Agent Compute Engine, announced for preview, which gives every agent its own isolated machine with no credentials inside and checks the user's delegation, the agent's identity and the machine's identity on every outbound call.[50] It ties each tool call to what happened inside the sandbox, but it does not record why the agent acted or whether the action fitted the case. That layer sits underneath decision engineering rather than replacing it.
  • Data platforms are positioning themselves as the context layer. At its Build conference in 2026, Microsoft presented Fabric as the shared context layer for agents.[6] This approach organizes context around stored data in a data lake.
  • Analysts describe the components as separate trends. Gartner's data and analytics trends for 2026 list decision governance, AI governance platforms and agentic data streaming as three separate items. Gartner projects that data streaming for agentic AI will jump from under 15% of organizations in 2025 to over 60% by 2028. It also predicts that explicitly modeled decisions will be five times more trusted than ungoverned decisions by 2029.[7] In June 2025 Gartner predicted that half of all business decisions will be augmented or automated by AI agents for decision intelligence by 2027.[8] In January 2026 it published its first Magic Quadrant for Decision Intelligence Platforms.
  • Model vendors are shipping decision models. TypeSafe AI released Jev on September 15, 2026 and called it a System One model. It returns a choice, a score or a probability from answers defined in advance, in one pass, and generates no text.[15] OpenAI previewed a Decisions API at its developer conference on September 29, 2026 and opened it to all developers in public beta on October 6, positioning it for classifying content, routing requests and choosing an agent's next action.[16] Both are deciders of the model kind described in post 5: they take the routine share of decisions over free text, which until now needed a language model agent, and they return a probability that the decision record keeps apart from the outcome.
  • Agent pricing is moving from activity to outcomes. Advertising went from paying per impression, to per click, to per sale, and each step only worked once buyers could verify the result. Agent pricing is on the same path. Salesforce Agentforce charges per conversation or per action, whether or not the problem gets solved.[23] Intercom charges $0.99 for each outcome its Fin agent delivers, counted when the customer asks for nothing more after Fin’s last answer,[21] and Zendesk bills per automated resolution, which a separate language model verifies after the conversation ends.[22] The argument is now about what counts as an outcome, and the old games are coming back: an agent can “resolve” a case by wearing the customer down, which is the agent version of click fraud. Paying for outcomes needs evidence that ties each decision to its confirmed result, which is what the decision record and the sixth trust property, “was it a good decision?”, provide. It also means the vendor’s margin depends on routing each case to the cheapest decider that’s good enough. Every outcome-priced vendor grades its own work, and Salesforce agreed to buy Fin in June 2026, so the grader and the platform are now the same company.[40] Insurers have noticed: AIUC-1 recertifies agents quarterly,[38] and Armilla’s Lloyd’s-backed policy covers “incorrect decisions, improper tool use, or escalation errors.”[39] The evaluation record is the neutral artifact, and the same record is the invoice basis, the chargeback evidence, the underwriting file and the audit trail.
  • Standards bodies are addressing agent identity. The US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) launched its AI Agent Standards Initiative in February 2026, covering security, interoperability and identity.[10] The second-quarter update of the AIUC-1 standard for agentic AI security separated agent identity and agent access into distinct control domains.[11] Agent identity that works from end to end is still being worked out; NIST published a concept paper on agent identity and authority in February 2026 and asked for public input.[9]

My reading of these developments is that they are converging from different starting points. Streaming vendors are adding governance, agent platforms are adding control, data platforms are adding context and cloud providers are adding isolated runtimes, while analysts still describe decisions, governance and streaming as three separate markets. The components are established: event streaming, business rules, decision modeling, workflow engines and governance tooling each have a decade or more of practice behind them. The contribution of this series is to integrate them around the business decision as the unit of accountability.

10The gap

Where today's capabilities stop

Most enterprises already own several of the pieces described in this series. Each solves an important part of the puzzle, and each stops short on its own:

CapabilityStrengthWhat it does not provide on its own
Lakehouses and data warehousesHistory, analytics, model training and governance of stored data. Many now ingest data in near real time.They are organized around stored data and its analysis, and some now serve low-latency workloads. They do not by themselves hold a decision in progress or an action awaiting authorization across the systems involved.
Agent frameworks and harnessesMaking an agent reliable. Many now persist state and can resume long-running work.That state belongs to one framework and one application. Agents built on different frameworks do not automatically share a record, a view of the facts or a set of limits.
Durable workflow enginesLong-running state, retries and compensation within one workflowEach engine keeps a detailed record of its own workflows. These engines complement the log, but evidence across independent engines, agents and systems of record still has to be integrated.
Agent protocols: MCP and Agent2Agent (A2A)Standard ways for an agent to reach tools and other agents, including how a caller is authenticated and authorizedSecurity and authorization depend on how each is implemented and deployed. Neither protocol by itself establishes a chain of accountability for a decision across agents, tools and organizations, or records what resulted from a call.
AI governance and observability toolsInventory, evaluation, monitoring and compliance reportingThey may not enforce every transaction in the path to the system of record, and diagnostic traces, where they are sampled, do not amount to complete evidence.
Integration, API management and process automationReliable, governed access to systems of recordThey already provide substantial authorization and audit, and were designed for predefined paths rather than a caller that plans its own route. They need extending for per-agent delegated authority, case scope and business-state evidence. They are the starting point for the action gateway, once agent identity, delegated authority, the idempotency ledger and the decision record are added, with enforcement points beside the systems whose latency or availability requires them.
Decision intelligence platformsModeling, versioning and governing decisionsThey can model, govern and execute decisions. What distinguishes this design is the shared, event-driven record spanning different kinds of decider and the systems that execute their actions.
Event streaming on its ownMoving and processing data in real timeIt is a data platform without a model of a decision. It can carry decision records but has no knowledge of what a decision is.

The first and last rows need each other. A streaming platform can make decisions in milliseconds, but without a lakehouse it has nowhere to train and improve its models. A lakehouse can learn from years of history, but live decisions happen outside it, for many systems at once. You need both loops, and you still have to add the decision controls and the connections to core systems.

These capabilities contribute where the requirements justify them, and none of them should be replaced. What they do not provide automatically is a single model of accountability, centered on the decision, that spans different agents, data platforms, workflows and systems of record. Building that model on top of them is the engineering work this series describes.

14The position

How this differs, and where to start

This series does not propose a new model, agent framework or data platform. It proposes connecting the technologies that enterprises already use around the business decisions they must make, carry out and account for. Four characteristics distinguish the framework from the approaches described earlier in this post.

  • The framework is organized around decisions, where most discussion to date has concerned agents. Decisions create the consequences for the business, and they are what the auditor and the regulator examine. An agent is only one of four kinds of decider, and in the worked example the deciders that handle the smallest share of the decision evaluations carry the most cost. That is why the decision, not the agent, is the unit of accountability.
  • Trust is defined in measurable terms. Each of the six properties has a mechanism and a measure, so a technical reader can test whether a given system meets the definition.
  • Three markets are treated as one architecture, because decision governance, AI governance and data streaming are connected through the decision record. Workflow engines and decision intelligence platforms already have decisions and governance of their own. What they do not produce is a common record of accountability and execution evidence that spans platforms, agents and systems of record, and that record is what this architecture adds.
  • The framework does not assume that every decision needs an agent. It states which decisions should be given to an agent and what must be in place before that happens.

What the engineering work involves

Confluent, now part of IBM, provides the real-time foundation of this architecture, but a platform alone does not deliver trusted decisions. Decision engineering is a discipline that is applied to a client's own processes and existing platforms, and no single product provides it. The table sets out the engineering work involved.

In my own work, the tools described in this series come together in IBM Process Studio, to which my team has contributed, and Context Studio, both part of IBM Enterprise Advantage.[20] Process Studio is where processes are developed and their decisions are designed, run and governed; Context Studio organizes, connects and prepares the data that gives agents their business context. The architecture itself does not depend on either, and the same approach applies to the platforms a client already runs.

CapabilityTechnology foundationThe engineering work
Real-time contextConfluent, with Apache Kafka, Apache Flink and change data captureConnects enterprise data sources, defines data contracts and engineers context that deciders can rely on
Decision design and routingRules engines, models, optimization solvers and agent platformsIdentifies the decisions in a process, models and versions them, routes each to the right kind of decider and evaluates the results
Controlled executionIntegration and API management, identity and workflow platformsDesigns the action gateway: enforcement of policy, safe commitment of resources, authorization and recovery
Trust and governanceIdentity, governance, observability and audit technologiesEstablishes decision lineage, reconciliation with systems of record, audit controls mapped to the regulations that apply, the agent registry and the operating model for oversight
AdoptionThe client's existing business and IT platformsIntegrates the architecture with the client's operating model, controls, release processes and business ownership

The next question is who does what. A decision owner in the business is accountable for each decision, its limits and its measures; where a decision spans departments, one of them owns it. An agent owner answers for each agent definition and its retirement. The platform team runs the log, the gateway and the registries, and owns no business decision. Risk approves each move up the autonomy scale, and operations takes the page when a guardian fires. In financial services, the agent and decision registries extend the model inventory that model risk management already keeps, and they fill a gap: the US banking regulators’ April 2026 model risk guidance leaves generative and agentic AI out of scope while saying governance must still cover them.[25]

Finding the first decision

The first question in any rollout is which decisions are actually worth delegating. Rarely is there a master list. Most decisions live in experienced employees' heads, legacy code, spreadsheets or existing prompts. Hunting them down takes a couple of weeks and four places to look:

  • Walk the process with the people who run it. Ask where someone has to choose: approve or decline, hold or release, which option, how much. Every "well, it depends" is a decision.
  • Follow the work queues. Exception queues, approval steps, manual overrides and rework show where decisions already wait for a person, and how many arrive each day.
  • Read the systems. Business rules in code and configuration, thresholds in workflow tools and the instructions in existing prompts are decisions someone has already made explicit, usually without an owner or a version.
  • Trace the events and logs. Wherever a record changes state, such as a claim moving to approved or a ticket being reissued, something decided it. The history shows the volume, the timing and how often the outcome was later reversed.

A language model can speed this up: it can read the process documents, logs and code and propose a first list far faster than a workshop can. It can propose, but it cannot settle business authority, acceptable risk or the right decider, so the business owner reviews every line and accepts or changes it.

The result is one line per decision, with the criteria on which the proposed decider rests.

CriterionWhat is recordedWhy it matters for the decider
Decision and ownerThe name of the decision, the process it belongs to and the business ownerEvery decision has an accountable owner before it is automated
Proposed deciderA rule, a model or solver, an agent or a person, with the reason for the choiceRouting sends each decision to the least expensive competent decider
Volume and deadlineEvaluations per day and the time available before the outcome mattersHigh volume with a short deadline favors rules and models
Reversibility of actionsEach action classified as reversible, compensable or irreversibleIrreversible actions need stronger approval, whichever decider takes them
Inputs and freshnessEach input, its system of record and the age it can have when usedShows whether the decision can be made on current facts
Real-time benefitWhere a decision made on live events, rather than on a nightly batch or a lookup at the moment of the request, would change the outcome, and by how muchShows which decisions need the event backbone first, and which can wait
Additional data setsData outside the process that would improve the decision, such as customer history, weather or capacity, with the reason each one helpsShows where a decision lacks context, and whether the gain is worth the cost of a new feed
Structure of the inputWhether the input is structured data, free text, or a case that involves another partyFree text with a known set of answers, such as the category of a message, points to a decision model. Free text that needs a reply or a plan, negotiation with another party or a case that needs reasoning across systems points to a language model agent. Structured input with a stated rule or objective points to a rule, a model or a solver.
Consequence of an errorThe estimated cost of a wrong decision and who bears itSets the level of review and the place in the rollout order
Existing controlsApprovals, reconciliations and audits already in placeAvoids duplicating controls and reveals gaps
Candidate measuresThe business measures that apply to the decisionProvides the baseline that the first 30 days require

The first 90 days

Before the clock starts, four things need to exist, or the first 30 days become the project of discovering that they don’t: events from the systems the decision touches, or change data capture to produce them; an identity provider that can issue identities to software, not only to people; permission to put an enforcement point in front of the system of record; and a business owner who will accept the baseline and defend it later.

Many operations start at level 1 on the autonomy scale in the brief, with live information in front of people who decide. Ninety days is a realistic target for proving the approach on a single, carefully scoped decision, typically moving it from level 2 (recommend) to level 3 (supervised), provided that the data, the access to systems and a business owner are in place. The decision should have high volume, a clear owner and a measurable outcome, such as rebooking after a missed connection, claim triage or a change to a credit line.

  1. Days 1 to 30: baseline and designList the candidate decisions and their proposed deciders, as described above, then select one decision and its owner. Record the baseline for each business measure listed in post 1, including decision latency and governance latency. Classify the risks and the actions involved, and design the architecture.
  2. Days 31 to 60: engineering and validationPublish the inputs as events with data contracts. Publish a decision record for every decision, even while people still make it. Enforce policy at the gateway, and run the new deciders in parallel with the existing process.
  3. Days 61 to 90: controlled automationGive the routine share of the decision to rules and models, and give agents limited authority over the difficult cases. A pilot with zero incidents on routine cases does not prove that the controls work. Before an agent receives broader authority, it must pass chaos tests that deliberately introduce stale data, race conditions, dropped events and unavailable downstream APIs.

Authority is extended only when six gates are passed. They test whether this implementation is ready for more autonomy; they are not the six trust properties of post 7, though two gates draw on them. Most pair a measurement from the 90 days with the chaos tests above. Being able to replay a decision is necessary evidence, but replay alone isn't enough to earn an agent more authority.

GateWhat passing it shows
Faster completed decisionsThe time from a business event to a confirmed action in the system of record has fallen against the baseline
Better decisionsErrors, rework, overrides and losses are lower than the baseline, and the stated confidence of predictions matches the results
Controlled autonomyNo unauthorized action was committed during operation or in the negative tests that were run, and every breach in those tests was blocked before execution
Safe recoveryDuplicate requests, interrupted processes and unavailable systems did not create inconsistent commitments, and compensating actions worked when tested
Complete evidenceEvery decision and action in scope can be reconciled independently with the systems of record, with no action found that lacks a record, and a deliberately introduced policy violation was detected within the agreed time
ValueThe measured benefits on the pilot volume, and the stated assumptions needed to project them to full volume, support a cost that covers the platform, the integration, the operation and the human oversight

The 90 days end with four results: a measured comparison with the baseline, evidence that the agreed control tests passed, an assessment of the risks still open and a recommendation on which decisions to expand to next. A successful first implementation also leaves behind reusable data contracts, decision definitions, integration patterns, protocols and tests, which reduce the effort needed to automate the next decision.

What actually goes wrong in first projects, without names: the decision owner turned out to be a committee that had never met; the change data capture from a core system took longer than the pilot; the business rules existed in four versions, one of them in the memory of someone who had retired; and one team kept a direct connection to the reservation system “for emergencies” and used it twice a week. None of these are technology failures, which is why the plan starts with a baseline and an owner rather than an agent.

Production is not the end of decision engineering. Business policies change, new information becomes available and decision quality can deteriorate. The same records and controls let teams measure those changes, test alternatives and improve decisions without rebuilding each process.

Where to begin

A first conversation needs four things: one candidate decision, the person who owns it, the systems it touches and the measure by which the business will judge it. The decision inventory above produces the candidates, and the 90-day plan above is how I would take the first one from baseline to controlled automation, using the tools described in this series. Those 90 days produce a measured result on one decision and an ordered list of decisions to automate next, which gives an enterprise program a firmer basis than a platform choice made first.

From hundreds to thousands

This series has addressed the step to hundreds of agents within one operation. The step to thousands will come when agents are used across every process of the enterprise and when partners, suppliers and customers bring agents of their own. The same principles should apply at that scale, with additional controls for scale and for trust across organizations. The additional work lies in the federated trust described in post 7, because an enterprise will then depend on agents that it did not build and cannot inspect. The method stays the same: begin with one well-scoped decision, run it in parallel, extend authority only on tested performance and approved controls, and treat the partners' agents as parties whose offers are verified, not trusted.

What this series established. A first engagement does not prove the architecture; it proves one decision at one level of autonomy. In 90 days it establishes four things: whether decision latency and governance latency fell against a measured baseline; whether the controls held when deliberately broken; which risks remain open; and whether the next decision is worth automating. Everything in the nine posts exists to make that first result credible, and everything after it is earned one decision at a time.

Talk to me

Talk to me

If you have a candidate decision and want a second opinion on the owner, the decider or the measure, send it to me. The decision inventory above is what my team runs with clients in the first weeks of a project, and I am happy to argue about yours. The easiest way to reach me is LinkedIn.

Coming next

Topics for future posts

This series has set out the framework, the worked example and the first 90 days. Several subjects deserve a post of their own, and the following are planned. Testing comes first, because controls need to be challenged under realistic failures before agents are given more authority.

TopicWhat the post will cover
Testing trusted decisionsHow to make the controls fail on purpose before agents are given authority: stale context, duplicate commitments, approval races, missing events, unavailable systems and runaway loops, and how the results feed the 90-day gates
Capturing decisions from existing systemsHow agent frameworks, workflow engines and cloud agent gateways publish the open decision record, so that systems already in place become sources of evidence without being rebuilt
Building the action gatewayThe gateway of post 6 in detail: policy in an open policy language (a vendor-neutral way to write rules as code), conditional commitment, the ledger for safe repetition, limits on causal chains and deployment as enforcement points beside each system
The trust scorecardA live view of the six trust properties for each type of decision, and how the gates for extending an agent's autonomy are read from it
Context from the decision streamTurning the history of decisions and their outcomes into context that is served back to deciders, and how evaluated feedback becomes approved changes to models and policies
Tamper-evident evidenceLinking decision records so that any alteration shows, keeping an independent copy, and verifying the archive against the regulations that apply
Dynamic harnesses, fixed controlsHarnesses that write and rewrite themselves at runtime, with a second system breaking them on purpose, are the next step in harness engineering. Why the gateway, the limits and the record must stay outside that loop, and how the chaos catalog becomes a breaker that runs continuously in production
What happens next

Bring one decision, its owner, the systems it touches and the measure the business will judge it by, and tell me about it. If you need the five-minute version for the people who approve the budget, it is the first tab.
